elements.text:
The proud man lives in fear of failure, and his anxiety comes from trying to hold up a false image. The humble man knows his value comes from God and rests in His assurance.
Dietrich Bonhoeffer

Pride is not thinking too much of yourself; it’s thinking of yourself too much. Anxiety follows when we are obsessed with our own significance.
Tim Keller

elements.question: John is in his early 30s ...
elements.answer:
John came to faith at 27. He is married 8 years, has 2 kids and joined his church 6 years ago. Recently he started a new job with a probationary period, but 6 months in anxiety hits. He isn’t sleeping or eating well; he doesn’t know why he’s anxious.

John is heavily involved in church, he prays and reads his Bible often. He notices where help is needed, even when others don’t, and he will get stuff done; he is a hard worker.

John is a chronic nail biter. He remembers having stopped for nearly 4 months, but then he had a job interview he really wanted, and the stress started everything again. He hasn’t stopped since.

John has a problem with porn. It was a struggle when he was first saved and it got better, although it still causes temptations, especially at more stressful times in life: deadlines in work, or maybe a bible study to prepare. He also talks about shouting at his children, finding parenting hard at times. He is constantly asking them to do the same things. His temper boils over a little too much for his liking.

For John school was difficult, he had a tough time with bullies and just wanting to fit in. He quickly went from girlfriend to girlfriend, rarely being outside of a relationship.

At home John recalls a difficult relationship with his mother, they never got along. He had a good relationship with his uncle, his mother’s brother. As a teenager he went to work most summers with him. He remembers his uncle once having and accident, breaking his wrist and being told to take it easy. This was during the school Easter holidays. John went to help him for 2 weeks, he was around 15 years old. He felt good because on the trip home his mother said, ‘I was told you worked really hard, well done.’

One other memory was when doing homework, John struggled with English and his mother got angry. He was around 12 years old, and clearly remembers his mother asking why he wasn’t as smart as the neighbour’s children. When asked about himself, John never talks about his good qualities. He focuses on the bad.

elements.text: The original human Fall in Genesis 3 is often connected with the foundational sin of pride. Adam and Eve listen to the serpent’s temptation to seek to be ’like God’ in a way that they shouldn’t be. They are already like God in every way that counts - they have been created in his image. But they think this is not enough.

elements.passageText: <sup>12</sup> Look how you have fallen from the sky, O shining one, son of the dawn! You have been cut down to the ground, O conqueror of the nations! <sup>13</sup> You said to yourself, “I will climb up to the sky. Above the stars of El I will set up my throne. I will rule on the mountain of assembly on the remote slopes of Zaphon. <sup>14</sup> I will climb up to the tops of the clouds; I will make myself like the Most High!” <sup>15</sup> But you were brought down to Sheol, to the remote slopes of the pit. <sup>16</sup> Those who see you stare at you, they look at you carefully, thinking: “Is this the man who shook the earth, the one who made kingdoms tremble? <sup>17</sup> Is this the one who made the world like a desert, who ruined its cities, and refused to free his prisoners so they could return home?”’

elements.question: How does human pride echo Satan’s own pride
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: Satan's fall in this passage is driven by a string of 'I will' statements — I will climb to the sky, I will set up my throne above the stars, I will make myself like the Most High. That's the shape of pride: not just an inflated view of self, but a desire to occupy God's place and rule apart from him. Human pride works the same way in miniature — every time we insist on being our own authority, or picture ourselves at the center where God belongs, we're echoing that same claim. And the passage's ending is a warning: the one who tried to rise above everyone else is instead brought down to the pit.
elements.questionHint: Count how many times the phrase 'I will' appears in verses 13-14 — what is each 'I will' aiming at?

elements.passageText: <sup>2</sup> “Son of man, say to the prince of Tyre, ‘This is what the sovereign Lord says: “‘Your heart is proud and you said, “I am a god; I sit in the seat of gods, in the heart of the seas” – yet you are a man and not a god, though you think you are godlike. <sup>3</sup> Look, you are wiser than Daniel; no secret is hidden from you. <sup>4</sup> By your wisdom and understanding you have gained wealth for yourself; you have amassed gold and silver in your treasuries. <sup>5</sup> By your great skill in trade you have increased your wealth, and your heart is proud because of your wealth. <sup>6</sup> “‘Therefore this is what the sovereign Lord says: Because you think you are godlike, <sup>7</sup> I am about to bring foreigners against you, the most terrifying of nations. They will draw their swords against the grandeur made by your wisdom, and they will defile your splendor. <sup>8</sup> They will bring you down to the pit, and you will die violently in the heart of the seas. <sup>9</sup> Will you still say, “I am a god,” before the one who kills you – though you are a man and not a god – when you are in the power of those who wound you? <sup>17</sup> Your heart was proud because of your beauty; you corrupted your wisdom on account of your splendor. I threw you down to the ground; I placed you before kings, that they might see you.

elements.question: How else does human pride echo Satan’s own pride
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: This time pride shows up wrapped in real ability — wisdom, wealth, and beauty. The prince of Tyre isn't imagining talents he doesn't have; he really was skilled in trade and impressive to look at. But he takes credit for what he has and lets it convince him he's above judgment, going so far as to say 'I am a god.' Verse 17 traces this straight back to beauty: his heart became proud simply because of how he looked. Like Satan, his gifts became the very thing he worshiped instead of the God who gave them, and the passage says that self-deification ends the same way — brought down and killed by foreigners.
elements.questionHint: What does the prince credit himself for in verses 4-5, and what does he end up saying about himself in verse 9?

elements.text: People over-reach themselves, and desire to be more than they are, more than they should be, and more than they can be. This is self-aggrandisement on the largest scale, pride at its most foundational.

elements.passageText: <sup>5</sup> The Lord abhors every arrogant person; rest assured that they will not go unpunished.

elements.question: Why is pride dangerous?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: This proverb doesn't soften the point: pride isn't just unattractive to God, it's something he abhors — a strong word, more than mere disapproval. And the second half closes off any hope of getting away with it: 'rest assured they will not go unpunished.' Pride is dangerous because it invites God's own opposition, and Scripture promises that opposition doesn't stay silent forever. It's not a minor character flaw to manage with a little humility talk; it's a stance toward God himself that he has committed to answering.
elements.questionHint: What specific word does this verse use for God's reaction to arrogance, and what does the second half promise will eventually happen?

elements.passageText: <sup>6</sup> But he gives greater grace. Therefore it says, “ God opposes the proud , but he gives grace to the humble .”

elements.question: Why else is pride dangerous?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: James puts pride and grace in direct opposition. The proud person isn't neutral before God — verse 6 says God actively opposes them, taking up a stance against them rather than simply withholding blessing. That's a sobering position to be in. But the flip side is just as real: grace flows to the humble. Pride is dangerous because it puts a person on the wrong side of that line, cutting them off from the very grace they need, while humility is what actually opens the door to receive it.
elements.questionHint: What verb does James use for what God does toward the proud — and what does he give instead to the humble?

elements.text: This foundational sin of pride, and bias towards self-aggrandisement, is then inherited by the subsequent generations of humanity that follow from Genesis 4 onwards. We are born biased towards selfishness, pride, and self-aggrandisement. But, this is not the full story. Precisely because our pride is over-reaching, it does not match up well with the situation in which we find ourselves.

elements.passageText: <sup>18</sup> Pride goes before destruction, and a haughty spirit before a fall.

elements.question: Why is it wise to avoid pride?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: The proverb sets up a sequence: pride comes first, and destruction follows after it, the way a haughty spirit precedes a fall. It's not that pride might occasionally lead somewhere bad — the proverb states it as a pattern built into how pride works. A haughty spirit clouds judgment, ignores warnings, and refuses correction, which is exactly the posture that sets someone up to trip. Avoiding pride is wise simply because it's avoiding the first domino in a chain that reliably ends in a fall.
elements.questionHint: What two things does the proverb say come 'before' something else — pride before what, and a haughty spirit before what?

elements.text: Humanity before the Fall is in a state of ’independent dependence’ - they are finite creatures dependent on an infinite God, but within that ultimate dependence they have great independence. They are to rule the cosmos as those who are the very image of God. This is a wide-ranging task, involving tremendous responsibility - and involves facing a massive, untamed creation - but they are equipped to undertake the task because their functional independence is rooted in foundational dependence on God. Their freedom is a rooted freedom.

elements.passageText: <sup>1</sup> If the Lord does not build a house, then those who build it work in vain. If the Lord does not guard a city, then the watchman stands guard in vain.

elements.question: How do we see that ’independent dependence’ at work in Scripture?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: This psalm holds two things together without erasing either. The builders still have to build, and the watchman still has to stay awake and watch — nobody is being told to sit back and do nothing. That's the 'independent' part: real, active human effort. But the psalm says plainly that without the Lord, all of that labor is 'in vain.' The work matters, but it isn't self-sufficient; its success depends entirely on something the workers themselves can't supply. That's the dependence — not less effort, but effort that knows it isn't the ultimate cause of its own success.
elements.questionHint: The builders and the watchman are still working hard in this psalm — so what exactly does the psalm say their labor depends on to not be 'in vain'?

elements.passageText: <sup>12</sup> So then, my dear friends, just as you have always obeyed, not only in my presence but even more in my absence, continue working out your salvation with awe and reverence, <sup>13</sup> for the one bringing forth in you both the desire and the effort – for the sake of his good pleasure – is God.

elements.question: How else do we see that ’independent dependence’ at work in Scripture?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: Paul tells the Philippians to keep working out their salvation — an active, ongoing task he expects them to do. But in the very next breath he says the desire to do it and the effort to carry it out both come from God working in them. That's the same pattern as before: real human effort that is nonetheless entirely dependent, down to the will to try in the first place. You don't get to skip the working, but you also can't credit the working to yourself, since even the wanting-to came from somewhere beyond you.
elements.questionHint: Paul tells them to 'work out' their salvation — but where does he say the desire and the effort to do that actually come from?

elements.text: The Fall shatters this situation of rooted freedom. After the Fall, we retain a great deal of freedom, but our freedom is now unrooted and cast adrift. We still face a massive, untamed creation, but now that creation is often hostile (sometimes lethally so). We have cast ourselves adrift from the resources, guidance, and wisdom of an infinite God, and thrown ourselves onto our own finite resources instead.

elements.passageText: <sup>5</sup> The Lord says, ’I will put a curse on people who trust in mere human beings, who depend om mere flesh and blood for their strength, and whose hearts have turned away from the Lord. <sup>6</sup> They will be like a shrub in the desert. They will not experience good things even when they happen. It will be as though they were growing in the desert, in a salt land where no one can live.’

elements.question: Why does it make a kind of sense to respond to the world with anxiety?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: If your security is built on 'mere human beings' or 'mere flesh and blood,' then anxiety is actually the appropriate response — that foundation genuinely can't hold. People fail, get sick, change their minds, and eventually die, so trusting them for your strength is like planting yourself as 'a shrub in the desert.' The image is vivid: parched, alone, unable to even notice good things when they arrive because you're surviving in salt land where nothing can really live. Anxiety makes sense here because the passage isn't describing an irrational fear — it's describing the natural result of depending on something too fragile to bear the weight.
elements.questionHint: What two things does the curse fall on trusting in, and what does the shrub-in-the-desert image suggest about depending on those things?

elements.passageText: <sup>1</sup> But understand this, that in the last days difficult times will come. <sup>2</sup> For people will be lovers of themselves, lovers of money, boastful, arrogant, blasphemers, disobedient to parents, ungrateful, unholy, <sup>3</sup> unloving, irreconcilable, slanderers, without self-control, savage, opposed to what is good, <sup>4</sup> treacherous, reckless, conceited, loving pleasure rather than loving God. <sup>5</sup> They will maintain the outward appearance of religion but will have repudiated its power. So avoid people like these.

elements.question: Why else does it make a kind of sense to respond to the world with anxiety?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: Paul's list here is a realistic description of what people can actually be like — 'lovers of themselves,' 'treacherous,' 'without self-control,' even people who keep 'the outward appearance of religion' while having 'repudiated its power.' If this is genuinely what the 'last days' and the people in them can look like, then feeling uneasy about the world isn't paranoia, it's paying attention. Difficult times are named as a real feature of this age, not a rare exception. Anxiety makes a kind of sense because the world Paul describes really can be treacherous and self-serving, even when it wears a religious face.
elements.questionHint: What does Paul say some people will keep up the 'outward appearance' of, even while lacking its actual power — and what does that suggest about trusting appearances?

elements.text: We are often daunted in the face of the cosmos; our freedom falters and faints. It makes sense that fallen humans are fundamentally anxious: we know that we do not have life in ourselves, and yet we have cast ourselves on our own resources, in the face of a world that overwhelms us.

elements.passageText: <sup>33</sup> I have told you these things so that in me you may have peace. In the world you have trouble and suffering, but take courage – I have conquered the world.”

elements.question: What is the right response to this anxiety?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: Jesus doesn't deny the anxiety-inducing reality of the previous passages — he says plainly, 'in the world you have trouble and suffering.' The right response isn't pretending that's not true. Instead, he points to himself as the reason courage is possible in spite of it: 'in me you may have peace,' because 'I have conquered the world.' The peace isn't found by fixing the trouble or finding a safer foundation among people or circumstances — it's found in a person who has already won the very conflict causing the trouble. Anxiety meets its answer not in denial but in Christ's finished victory.
elements.questionHint: Jesus doesn't tell them the trouble isn't real — so what does he point to instead as the reason for taking courage?

elements.question: Tell John a better story ...
elements.answer:
Adult John needs to retell the story of his childhood. He needs to watch Jesus tell 12-year-old John a story about their heavenly Father who makes everyone special and unique, with different gifts, yet each is precious. Jesus says to young John:

Childhood is amazing for having fun and learning. As kids play and work, they find out what they are good at, what gifts God has given them. One day they will use those skills to bless others. Sometimes children struggle with this. They think everyone else’s gifts are better and get sad, or they think their gifts are the best and get proud. But gifts are as equally amazing as they are different. Enjoy your gifts and the gifts of everyone around you. The gifts are there for you to develop and enjoy and use to bring blessing to this broken world. Never be afraid to try stuff and fail, or to explore your gifts and make mistakes. You are exploring the person that God has made you, and He is delighted to see you try and fail and try again.

Sometimes when people are not feeling good about themselves, they say mean things to others. When someone says mean things like that to you, I want you to remember: it says more about how they are struggling than about you. I want to tell you a secret. Your mum is hurting. Someone has said mean things to her and she has said even meaner things to herself. She is feeling like a failure. She is hurting. And she is about to come over here and she wants to help you explore your gifts, but she can’t. And when she can’t, she is going to say something that she doesn’t believe and she doesn’t mean. And it will hurt. And it is something that no child should hear from their mother. And when she says it, I want you to see past her words and see her pain. This is not about you, it’s about her struggles. I want you to take the forgiveness I have given you and I want you to forgive her. She loves you. And even more, I love you. And you don’t need to be good at homework or anything else to get my love, you already have it, just look at the Cross - nothing could take my love from you. Now let’s sit here and try some more homework and together, we are going to explore your gifts and praise your father in heaven.

Those memories aren’t going away for adult John. They might be buried but what they need is the healing balm of the Gospel. Yes, John is guilty of disordered self-love, idolatry and pride. He needs to repent of seeking ultimate acceptance in the wrong places, but what he also needs is the Saviour. This is not a ’one time conversation.’ John will need to return to those childhood narratives many times, with Jesus by his side, telling a better, more truthful and gracious story.

elements.text:
Anxiety is often a byproduct of pride, where we think we must handle everything ourselves. In God’s hands, we find rest from both.
A.W. Tozer

Pride can mask itself as anxiety. We worry because we think we have to be in control. But when we humble ourselves, we learn to trust God with what we cannot manage.
Max Lucado

elements.question: Frank is in his mid-30s ...
elements.answer:
Frank is a Christian but struggles with identity, motivation and endurance in the Christian life. Frank was raised in a Christian home to caring parents. They lived in the countryside but were not farmers. His father was an outgoing people-person, who grew up in the town, and his mother an introverted countrywoman. He was the youngest child and grew up with little day to day interaction with anyone outside his family. He was taught not to be showy or proud but to quietly get on with life and to work hard. He trusted in Christ at an early age and was keen to please God at primary school which was very small.

In academic selection (at aged 11) Frank’s siblings did not perform as well as hoped. Frank did better than expected. This was awkward for his parents to handle and confusing for Frank who was glad he did well but began to internalise that success was a source of embarrassment. Frank opted, with his parent’s encouragement, to go to the same high school as his siblings rather than the local grammar school as it was thought that he wouldn’t cope there. Throughout the rest of his school life he found that doing well in school came relatively easily but success was always something to be kept quiet or to be embarrassed about, at home and in school.

In high school he fell between two groups of students: those raised in the farming community and those raised in the town (mostly from quite an aggressively loyalist area). Frank’s family lived in the countryside but were not farmers and so he felt he could not relate to either group.

As well as this, he was not maintaining a clear Christian witness and so maintained a lingering guilt. He had a feeling of not being comfortable either in his own skin or with those around him. He became afraid of saying or doing the wrong thing socially. Towards the end of high school the gospel began working on his heart; he began to be freed from the fear of man and started to follow Christ more closely. He began to serve in his church and on summer teams.

After university and entering the working world he began with great hope for achievement and growth in his own life and in his work. The reality was, however, much more difficult and slow. There were many setbacks. He became afraid of failure and grew happy to just coast and please the people around him. Ambition and adventure in life became viewed as a suspicious source of pride or as too dangerous in case he fails.

He struggles with self-discipline and establishing routines in his life. He recognises his lack of assertiveness over both his own life and his career and yet struggles to gain control. This in turn leads to further frustration and resignation.

elements.text: Fallen humanity is biased towards two foundational attitudes: pride (seeking to be like God in all the wrong ways), and anxiety (realising that we are ill-equipped to face a disordered universe in our own strength). By default, we live with a sinful tension: we want to be gods and we realise we are not strong enough to be the gods we want to be(!)

elements.passageText: <sup>5</sup> “I am the vine; you are the branches. The one who remains in me – and I in him – bears much fruit, while one who does not bear fruit shows that he does not have the life because apart from me you can accomplish nothing.

elements.question: What should we realise instead?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: Jesus draws a picture where the branch has no independent life of its own — its fruitfulness comes entirely from remaining connected to the vine. That's what we should realize instead of relying on our own strength or achievement: apart from him, the text says flatly, 'you can accomplish nothing.' Not less, not a diminished version — nothing. Whatever fruit does appear in a life comes from staying attached to Christ, not from personal effort generating results independently. The proper response to pride isn't just trying harder; it's recognizing where the life and fruitfulness were actually coming from all along.
elements.questionHint: What does Jesus say happens to fruit-bearing 'apart from me' — what specific word does he use for how much we can accomplish on our own?

elements.passageText: <sup>9</sup> But he said to me, “My grace is enough for you, for my power is made perfect in weakness.” So then, I will boast most gladly about my weaknesses, so that the power of Christ may reside in me.

elements.question: What else should we realise instead?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: Paul had asked God to remove a weakness, and the answer he gets isn't the removal he wanted but a reframing: God's power is 'made perfect in weakness,' not in spite of it. What we should realize instead of chasing strength and self-sufficiency is that weakness is actually the place where Christ's power shows up most clearly. That's why Paul says he'll boast 'most gladly' about his weaknesses — not out of forced positivity, but because he's seen that his own limits are exactly where Christ's power comes to reside in him. Weakness stops being something to hide and becomes the very place strength is found.
elements.questionHint: What does Paul say happens to Christ's power specifically 'in weakness' — and why does that change how he feels about boasting in his weaknesses?

elements.text: The right response to self, in the face of this combination of pride and anxiety, is not more focus on self. It does not help to get caught up in self-guilt or self-reproach, or self-loathing, or self-condemnation. That is just another way of getting stuck in the problem of self-focus. Instead, the right response is to turn to God in faith and repentance. This frees us to develop a well-ordered and humble self-love. After all, if God loves us, and if we are to be like God, then there is a right and proper way to humbly love ourselves. But if we don't find that way, then we will develop one of these two basic pathologies of self-love - everyday pride or everyday anxiety. (Or some variation of them, such as despair or apathy.)

elements.passageText: <sup>3</sup> For by the grace given to me I say to every one of you not to think more highly of yourself than you ought to think, but to think with sober discernment, as God has distributed to each of you a measure of faith.

elements.question: What is the antidote to this wrong thinking?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: Paul's antidote to pride isn't self-hatred or refusing to think about yourself at all — it's accurate thinking. He tells them not to think 'more highly' of themselves 'than you ought,' which implies there is an 'ought,' a true measure to be had. The corrective is 'sober discernment' — clear-eyed, unclouded judgment rather than either inflated or falsely deflated self-assessment. And he grounds that accurate view in something outside yourself: whatever faith or ability you have was 'distributed' to you by God. Sober thinking remembers that even your gifts are on loan, which leaves no room for either arrogance or despair.
elements.questionHint: What phrase does Paul use instead of 'don't think about yourself' — and where does he say the 'measure' each person has actually came from?

elements.text: We live in a broken world, as creatures estranged from our creator, and as guilty sinners who will one day give an account before our Judge. It is no surprise that we have a bent towards anxiety. The right response is to fix our eyes on God, in faith, repentance, and humility.

elements.passageText: <sup>3</sup> Instead of being motivated by selfish ambition or vanity, each of you should, in humility, be moved to treat one another as more important than yourself. <sup>4</sup> Each of you should be concerned not only about your own interests, but about the interests of others as well. <sup>5</sup> You should have the same attitude toward one another that Christ Jesus had, <sup>6</sup> who though he existed in the form of God did not regard equality with God as something to be grasped, <sup>7</sup> but emptied himself by taking on the form of a slave, by looking like other men, and by sharing in human nature. <sup>8</sup> He humbled himself, by becoming obedient to the point of death – even death on a cross!

elements.question: What does humility look like, and involve?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: Humility here has a specific shape: it's the opposite of being driven by 'selfish ambition or vanity,' and it shows up in action, not just as an inward feeling. Paul defines it as treating others 'as more important than yourself,' and being concerned not only for your own interests but for the interests of others too. That's a real redirection of attention — noticing and caring about what matters to someone else as much as what matters to you. And this humility isn't just a nice ideal Paul invents; he grounds it in Christ's own attitude, holding Jesus up as the pattern everyone else is meant to copy.
elements.questionHint: What two things does Paul say humility is NOT motivated by, and whose attitude does he point to as the pattern to copy?

elements.passageText: <sup>8</sup> He has told you, O man, what is good, and what the Lord really wants from you: he wants you to promote justice, to be faithful, and to live obediently before your God.

elements.question: What else does humility look like, and involve?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: Micah lists three things, not one: promote justice, be faithful, and live obediently before God. Humility here isn't reduced to feeling small — it's bound up with how you treat others (justice), how reliable you are (faithfulness), and the everyday posture of walking in step with God rather than out ahead of him or against him. 'Live obediently' captures what real humility looks like in practice: not just occasional acts of self-abasement, but a life continually ordered around what God wants rather than your own agenda. It's less a mood and more a direction the whole life travels in.
elements.questionHint: Micah names three specific things God wants — justice, faithfulness, and what third thing regarding how you live 'before your God'?

elements.text: If we do turn to Him, our anxiety is answered with reconciliation and peace, and our self-love is reset into humility. But as sinners, this is not our instinctive response. Instead we turn our gaze inwards, towards disordered self-love, and we trust in our self. We double-down on the mistake of pride and trust in the self that we want to be.

elements.passageText: <sup>17</sup> But the one who boasts must boast in the Lord. <sup>18</sup> For it is not the person who commends himself who is approved, but the person the Lord commends.

elements.question: Where should we be looking instead?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: Instead of looking to ourselves for validation, Paul redirects attention entirely: whatever boasting happens should be 'in the Lord,' not in personal achievement or comparison with others. He makes the point sharp by contrasting two kinds of approval — self-commendation carries no real weight, but being commended by the Lord is what actually counts. That flips where we naturally look for affirmation. Instead of building a case for ourselves and hoping others, or we ourselves, buy it, the passage says the only approval that matters is the one that comes from outside us, from God's own verdict.
elements.questionHint: Paul contrasts two people — the one who 'commends himself' and the one the Lord commends. Which one does he say is actually approved?

elements.text: This ’idealised self’ that we trust in will then lead us towards one of two concrete outcomes: everyday pride or everyday anxiety. If we think we are (broadly) succeeding at becoming our idealised self in practice, then we will take pride in our self, and our achievements, and we will use that everyday pride to suppress our sense of anxiety. This comes at a cost. As well as the normal ugliness of a prideful life, there is the cost of keeping on proving that we are our ideal self.

elements.passageText: The wicked man is so arrogant he always thinks, ’God won’t hold me accountable; he doesn’t care.’

elements.question: Why is pride so dangerous?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: This verse traces pride to its root belief: the arrogant person's constant inner assumption is that God won't hold him accountable, that God doesn't even care enough to notice. Pride is dangerous because it isn't just an attitude about yourself — it quietly rewrites your view of God, shrinking him into someone who's either absent or indifferent to what you do. Once that belief takes hold, there's nothing left to restrain behavior, because the very idea of accountability has been argued away. Pride's danger isn't just arrogance about self, it's the theology it smuggles in alongside it.
elements.questionHint: What two things does the arrogant person tell himself about God in this verse — and what would believing that free him to do?

elements.text: If we think we are (broadly) failing at becoming our idealised self in practice, then we will become increasingly anxious about our self, and our achievements - and that anxiety may lead us to despair. This also comes at a cost. As well as the normal stresses of an anxious life, we keep reminding ourselves of our failure to be our ideal self.

elements.passageText: <sup>6</sup> Do not be anxious about anything. Instead, in every situation, through prayer and petition with thanksgiving, tell your requests to God. <sup>7</sup> And the peace of God that surpasses all understanding will guard your hearts and minds in Christ Jesus.

elements.question: How does God call us to turn from anxiety?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: The turn from anxiety isn't willpower or simply deciding to stop worrying — Paul gives a specific action: bring your requests to God, 'through prayer and petition with thanksgiving,' 'in every situation.' Anxiety is met not with suppression but with speech — actually voicing what's worrying you to God, and doing it with gratitude woven in rather than only complaint. What follows isn't a guarantee that the situation resolves the way you hoped, but a peace that 'surpasses all understanding,' stationed like a guard over your heart and mind. The turn from anxiety runs through prayer, not around it.
elements.questionHint: What specific action does Paul tell them to do 'in every situation' instead of being anxious — and what does he say the resulting peace will do to 'guard'?

elements.text: Everyday pride and anxiety are opposites, but they are also closely connected, as different expressions of the same disordered self-love. Anxiety is an upside-down version of pride. We condemn ourselves for not achieving all that we want, because we have too grand a view of our own powers. Anxiety and pride are two sides of the same coin - which is why some people flip between the two. Others, if anxiety cannot be sedated, turn to self-apathy, an attempt at self-numbing.

elements.passageText: And God will exalt you in due time, if you humble yourselves under his might hand by casting all your cares on him because he cares for you.

elements.question: God calls us to a different life. What does that life look like?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: The different life Peter describes has two movements that go together: humbling yourself under God's mighty hand, and casting your cares onto him. Those aren't separate tasks — humility is expressed precisely by handing your anxieties over rather than carrying them yourself as if you had to manage everything. And the reason given for doing this isn't stoic resignation, it's relational: 'because he cares for you.' The promise attached is exaltation 'in due time' — not immediately, and not by your own striving, but as something God does for the humble when the time is right. It's a life of active trust rather than self-reliant control.
elements.questionHint: What single action does Peter say humbling yourself under God's hand actually looks like — and what reason does he give for why you can do that?

elements.question: Tell Frank a better story ...
elements.answer:
Frank needs to retell that story of his childhood, to have Jesus take 11-year-old Frank by the hand and celebrate his academic achievement, to explain to him that his parents are trying to protect him. He needs Jesus to explain to 11-year-old Frank that God has given him a wonderful gift to be used and celebrated and that God is going to equip little Frank with skills that are going to be a blessing in this broken world, that God’s grace in saving him from sin is the same amazing grace that sends him out in the name of Christ, confident that he is going to be used by God (Ephesians 2:8-10).

30-year-old Frank needs to watch Jesus take 11-year-old Frank by the hand and explain what happened. Assuming that Frank’s parents were trying to teach humility (rather than trying to suppress his gifts), 30-year-old Frank needs to watch Jesus talk to 11-year-old Frank, to assure him that his gifts are special and that he has been given them to be used and make a difference in this world, he needs to watch as Jesus encourages 11-year-old Frank to forgive his father, maybe not for wilfully trying to damage Frank but for missing the impact of his words.

30-year-old Frank needs to watch Jesus as he talks to 11-year-old Frank, as Jesus asks him about all he learnt in school and watch how Jesus smiles from ear to ear, celebrating the heavenly Father that gives every good gift (James 1).

As Frank’s affections are reordered, as he stops fearing that godly ambition equals pride and family rejection, as Jesus’ words start to bring healing to his self-understanding, then he may have the freedom to develop godly ambition and drive.

Edward has just initiated and completed a divorce. He had been married to Mary for 15 years and they have 2 children together. When they went through the divorce, he told Mary that he had known for a long time that he didn’t feel like he loved her. A few months after the divorce, Edward calls Mary to say he has made a mistake. His life is empty, he needs her back.

  • Edward loves the healthy lifestyle. He has a strict exercise routine, only eats healthy food, treats his body like a temple. Sometimes obsessively so.
  • He only had one long term girlfriend before he married Mary. He broke up with her for the same reason: he didn’t feel like he really loved her.
  • He absolutely loves his job; he is a lawyer and he is passionate about what he does. He has been very successful and has a reputation for getting what he wants, even if he has to be ruthless with people to get it.
  • Apart from their wedding day, Mary has no memory of them spending any time with Edward’s parents. Occasionally Edward talks about his Dad and has fond memories. He never talks about his Mum. If Mary ever pushed for information, Edward would just say that she was a hard woman and they have drifted apart.
  • Edward’s mother was an insecure, angry lady. Edward craved to be hugged and cared for. At age 9 Edward came home after being seriously bullied and his mother showed no compassion and told him that he probably deserved it.

elements.passageText: <sup>5</sup> Counsel in a person’s heart is like deep water, but an understanding person draws it out.

elements.question: Why is it hard to understand ourselves and others?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: The proverb compares what's inside a person to 'deep water' — not shallow or immediately visible, but something with real depth that takes effort to reach. That's why understanding ourselves and others is hard: our real motives, intentions, and 'counsel' aren't sitting on the surface where a glance can catch them. They have to be drawn out, like water pulled up from a well, which takes patience, attentiveness, and often the help of 'an understanding person' who knows how to ask the right questions. The heart doesn't advertise itself; it has to be drawn out on purpose.
elements.questionHint: What image does the proverb use for what's inside a person's heart, and what does it say is needed to actually 'draw it out'?

elements.text: Four clues can help us understand the loves at the centre of our hearts: desire, joy, fear, and sorrow. When we love something, we pursue it - we desire the joy of being satisfied by it. When we love something, we protect it - we fear the sorrow of losing it.

elements.passageText: <sup>5</sup> For those who live according to the flesh have their outlook shaped by the things of the flesh, but those who live according to the Spirit have their outlook shaped by the things of the Spirit.

elements.question: How do our desires and fears help reveal our hearts?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: Paul says our 'outlook' — the way we see and evaluate everything — gets shaped by whatever we're living according to. If it's the flesh, our thinking is shaped by 'the things of the flesh'; if it's the Spirit, it's shaped by 'the things of the Spirit.' That means desires and fears aren't just random impulses; they're diagnostic. What you desire and what you fear reveal what's actually shaping your outlook, because those things flow from whichever direction — flesh or Spirit — your life is oriented toward. Desires and fears function like a readout of what's really governing the heart underneath.
elements.questionHint: What does Paul say gets 'shaped' by whether someone lives according to the flesh or the Spirit — and what would your desires reveal about which one is doing the shaping?

elements.passageText: <sup>4</sup> “I tell you, my friends, do not be afraid of those who kill the body, and after that have nothing more they can do. <sup>5</sup> But I will warn you whom you should fear: Fear the one who, after the killing, has authority to throw you into hell. Yes, I tell you, fear him! <sup>7</sup> In fact, even the hairs on your head are all numbered. Do not be afraid; you are more valuable than many sparrows. <sup>32</sup> “Do not be afraid, little flock, for your Father is well pleased to give you the kingdom.

elements.question: How else do our desires and fears help reveal our hearts?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: Jesus assumes his listeners already fear something — the question is whether it's the right thing. He redirects their fear away from those who 'kill the body' toward the one with 'authority to throw you into hell,' which exposes what actually deserves to be feared versus what merely feels threatening. Then he undercuts ordinary anxiety altogether by pointing to how valued they are — more than 'many sparrows' — and by naming God as 'Father,' one who is 'well pleased' to give them the kingdom. Our fears reveal our hearts because they show what we actually believe has ultimate power over us and whether we trust the one behind that power.
elements.questionHint: Jesus tells them to fear one specific thing instead of physical death — what is it, and what does he call God right after, to reassure them?

elements.text: Desires are not bad; they are good, and it would be bad to lose them. We can desire wrong things, just like we can do wrong things - but the solution is not to desire nothing - that would make us less human, and more like a rock. Desires are part of how God created us.

elements.passageText: May he grant your heart’s desire; may he bring all your plans to pass!

elements.question: How do we know that having desires (and having them satisfied) is a good thing?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: This is offered as a blessing, not a warning — the psalmist prays that God himself would grant someone's heart's desire and bring their plans to pass. That tells us desire isn't inherently suspect in Scripture; having desires and plans, and wanting them fulfilled, is treated here as something worth asking God for on someone else's behalf. If desire were simply dangerous, this wouldn't be the kind of thing you'd pray as a blessing over a friend. Desire and its satisfaction are cast as gifts God gives, not just temptations he restrains.
elements.questionHint: Is this verse framed as a warning against desire or as something being prayed as a blessing over someone — what does that framing suggest about desire itself?

elements.passageText: <sup>2</sup> Praise the Lord , O my soul! Do not forget all his kind deeds! <sup>3</sup> He is the one who forgives all your sins, who heals all your diseases, <sup>4</sup> who delivers your life from the Pit, who crowns you with his loyal love and compassion, <sup>5</sup> who satisfies your life with good things, so your youth is renewed like an eagle’s.

elements.question: How else do we know that having desires (and having them satisfied) is a good thing?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: The psalmist calls his soul to remember God's 'kind deeds,' and the list that follows is a catalogue of desires actually being met: forgiveness, healing, deliverance, crowning with love, and satisfaction — the passage even names it directly, 'satisfies your life with good things.' God isn't shown here withholding good things or treating desire as a problem to manage; he's shown actively fulfilling it, to the point of renewal, 'like an eagle's' youth. If satisfied desire were dangerous, this whole psalm of praise would be praising the wrong thing — instead it treats being satisfied by God as exactly what deserves praise.
elements.questionHint: What specific verb does verse 5 use for what God does to 'your life' with good things — and how does the psalmist respond to that in verse 2?

elements.passageText: <sup>4</sup> Then you will take delight in the Lord, and he will answer your prayers.

elements.question: How do we know that having desires (and having them satisfied) is a good thing?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: This verse ties delighting in the Lord directly to having your desires met — the promise is that he 'will answer your prayers,' not that he'll teach you to stop wanting things. That's significant: desire and delight aren't presented as obstacles to spiritual maturity but as something God responds to. The verse doesn't ask you to suppress what you want; it points you toward delighting in God as the context in which real desires get real answers. Having desires satisfied is shown here as compatible with, even connected to, a life oriented toward delighting in the Lord.
elements.questionHint: What does the verse say happens to your prayers once you delight in the Lord — does it say desires get suppressed or answered?

elements.text: Fears and desires can often be connected to sin within us. If we are driven by pride and/or anxiety, then our desires and fears will be connected to that pride or anxiety. Thus, if someone’s desires are threatened, and/or their fears are triggered, pride or anxiety may colour the way they respond. This is not because desires and fears are wrong in principle. Desires and fears are good to have! We seek what we love, we long for it and pursue it. Desire begins the search. The stronger the love, the more intense the desire, the more relentless the search, the more satisfying the embrace. We desire what we love, and we feel joy as we move towards the objects of our desire.

elements.passageText: The righteousness of the upright will deliver them, but the faithless will be captured by their own desires. ... What the righteous desire leads only to good, but what the wicked hope for leads to wrath.

elements.question: Why can desires be a problem?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: These proverbs show desire isn't neutral — it's shaped by the kind of person having it, and it can turn on the person who holds it. The faithless aren't described as merely disappointed by their desires but 'captured' by them, as if desire becomes a trap that closes around someone who has no righteousness to deliver them from it. And the outcome tracks the source: what the righteous desire 'leads only to good,' while what the wicked hope for 'leads to wrath.' Desire is a problem when it's rooted in faithlessness or wickedness, because then the very thing you're chasing becomes what ends up holding you.
elements.questionHint: What verb does the first proverb use for what happens to the faithless because of their own desires — captured, or just disappointed?

elements.passageText: <sup>16</sup> But I say, live by the Spirit and you will not carry out the desires of the flesh. <sup>17</sup> For the flesh has desires that are opposed to the Spirit, and the Spirit has desires that are opposed to the flesh, for these are in opposition to each other, so that you cannot do what you want. ... <sup>24</sup> Now those who belong to Christ have crucified the flesh with its passions and desires.

elements.question: Why else can desires be a problem?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: Paul describes an internal war: the flesh has desires 'opposed to the Spirit,' and the Spirit has desires opposed to the flesh, and the effect of that conflict is that 'you cannot do what you want' — desire itself becomes unreliable, pulled in two directions at once. That's part of why desire is a problem: it isn't a simple, trustworthy compass, because there are competing desires at work inside a person. Paul's answer isn't to negotiate a truce but to say those who belong to Christ 'have crucified the flesh with its passions and desires' — the fleshly desires aren't managed, they're put to death.
elements.questionHint: What does Paul say happens to a person's ability to 'do what you want' when flesh and Spirit are in opposition — and what does he say Christians have done to the flesh's desires, rather than just resist them?

elements.passageText: <sup>11</sup> Dear friends, I urge you as foreigners and exiles to keep away from fleshly desires that do battle against the soul,

elements.question: Why else can desires be a problem?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: Peter frames the danger in military terms — fleshly desires 'do battle against the soul,' actively fighting to conquer something in you rather than sitting there harmlessly. That's a stronger claim than saying desires are just distracting; he's saying there's real combat happening, with the soul as the target. He also grounds his warning in identity: readers are addressed 'as foreigners and exiles,' people who don't ultimately belong to the world whose desires they're being warned about. Desires become a problem precisely when they wage this kind of war against who you actually are, rather than simply reflecting who you are.
elements.questionHint: What verb does Peter use for what fleshly desires do to the soul — and what two words does he use to describe the identity of the people he's warning?

elements.passageText: <sup>5</sup> So put to death whatever in your nature belongs to the earth: sexual immorality, impurity, shameful passion, evil desire, and greed which is idolatry.

elements.question: How should we deal with wrong desires?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: Paul's instruction is blunt and violent by design: 'put to death.' Not manage, not gradually outgrow, not simply resist in the moment — kill it. He lists 'evil desire' right alongside sexual immorality, impurity, and greed, treating wrong desire with the same seriousness as any other named sin, and he even calls greed 'idolatry,' worship misdirected toward something other than God. Dealing with wrong desires, in this passage, means a decisive, ongoing act of execution against whatever in you still 'belongs to the earth,' not a negotiation or a slow taming.
elements.questionHint: What verb does Paul use for what to do with these things — negotiate with them, manage them, or something more decisive?

elements.text: Fear and sorrow are mirror images of desire and joy. We fear the loss of the things that we love, and we experience sorrow if and when our fears are realised - if and when that loss occurs.

elements.passageText: <sup>17</sup> And if you address as Father the one who impartially judges according to each one’s work, live out the time of your temporary residence here in reverence.

elements.question: When is fear good, and when is it bad?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: Peter connects fear, rendered here as 'reverence,' to two things held together: calling God 'Father' and recognizing he 'impartially judges according to each one's work.' Good fear, in this sense, is the reverence that comes from taking seriously that the one you call Father is also the one who judges fairly, without favoritism — it shapes how you 'live out' your time here, keeping you honest rather than presumptuous. This isn't the fear of an enemy or a stranger; it's the reverence appropriate to someone who is both your Father and your impartial judge, which is exactly the combination that keeps fear healthy rather than terrifying.
elements.questionHint: What two roles does Peter combine for God in this verse — Father and what else — and how does holding both together shape 'reverence'?

elements.passageText: <sup>20</sup> For everyone who does evil deeds hates the light and does not come to the light, so that their deeds will not be exposed.

elements.question: When else is fear good, and when is it bad?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: This verse describes bad fear: fear of exposure. Someone doing evil 'hates the light' and avoids it, not because the light is harmful but because it would reveal what they're doing — the fear here is self-protective, aimed at keeping deeds hidden rather than at anything true about God. That's fear turned toward concealment instead of toward reverence. Unlike the healthy fear that leads someone to live rightly before a God who sees everything, this fear leads to avoidance, staying in the dark on purpose so the truth about one's deeds never comes to light.
elements.questionHint: What does the person in this verse actually fear — being seen doing wrong, or God himself — and what does that fear make them do?

elements.passageText: <sup>4</sup> Even when I must walk through the darkest valley, I fear no danger, for you are with me; your rod and your staff reassure me.

elements.question: How should we deal with wrong fears?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: The psalmist doesn't pretend the darkest valley isn't real or frightening — he names it directly. But the fear is dealt with not by denying the danger but by locating a presence stronger than the fear: 'you are with me.' That's the whole strategy here — not talking yourself out of the darkness, but trusting that God's presence, pictured in the rod and staff a shepherd uses to protect and guide, is reassurance enough to walk through it without being ruled by fear. Wrong fear is answered not with bravado but with the confidence that comes from not walking through the valley alone.
elements.questionHint: What reason does the psalmist give for not fearing danger — is it that the valley isn't actually dark, or is it something else that's present with him?

elements.passageText: Fearing the Lord is the beginning of moral knowledge, but fools despise wisdom and instruction.

elements.question: Who should we fear, and desire?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: The proverb answers directly: the Lord is the one to be feared, and that fear isn't a dead end but a starting point — 'the beginning of moral knowledge.' Real understanding of right and wrong doesn't start with clever reasoning on your own; it starts with rightly fearing God. The proverb then draws the contrast sharply: those who skip that fear become fools who 'despise wisdom and instruction,' rejecting the very thing that could have set them on the right path. Fearing the Lord, then, isn't just one virtue among many — it's the foundation everything else, including right desire, is meant to be built on.

elements.question: Edward’s fears and desires ...
elements.answer:
Despite what he said at the time, it seems Edward didn’t divorce Mary because of a lack of affection or desire for her, but because of his love for control, and his fear of emotional intimacy. Those desires and fears overshadowed his love for her (and his fear of loneliness). He believed that distancing himself from the relationship would solve his discomfort.

But once the divorce was final, Edward’s other fears - of isolation and loneliness - began to become dominant again, as did his love for Mary and their children. Without the relationship, his life felt empty, and he realised that Mary’s presence brought him a sense of stability and joy that he hadn’t fully appreciated. Edward’s call to Mary, months after the divorce, reveals a shift in the cycle of his desires. His need for control and distance is no longer in the driving seat, and he is becoming more and more conscious of his desire to reconcile and find meaning in the relationship he had discarded. He realises that his life feels incomplete without Mary and their children, and that the pursuit of his personal ambitions has left him unfulfilled.

However, unless Edward changes on a deeper level, he is likely to repeat the same cycle. Even if Mary took him back - or even if he eventually entered a relationship with someone else - unless he addresses the deep things going on in his heart, he will in time cycle back to his desire for control and fear of intimacy.

To move forward, Edward must confront the deep fears and desires that rule his life. He must learn to turn from them towards God as his foundation. His misshapen fears and desires flow from his disordered loves. He needs to understand that his desires can only be met in God, and his fears only overcome in God. Without correcting those foundations he will find it difficult to desire healthy relationships with others, and embrace vulnerability, rather than fear it. This will require repentance and a new understanding of how love works - not as a tool for control, but as a foundation of selfless connection, allowing his desires to be reshaped by God’s love and truth.

elements.question: Married, mid-30s
elements.answer:
Glen and Jennifer go to church. Jennifer comes across as a private person and doesn’t connect with many people at church. They don’t support the church financially and Jennifer hates always being asked to serve.

Glen’s Perspective: We’ve been married 5 years. I was attracted to Jennifer as she was so strong and driven and such a good mother to her son Bobby (he is 16). She says she doesn’t want any more children and won’t engage with the fact that I really do. It’s like she is always looking out for herself. She keeps her own savings account and even if things are tight, she’ll dip into it to go to a beauty salon, but I can’t touch it to help cover car repairs. She worked her way up to being the store manager at the local supermarket, but the rest of staff hate working for her. She micromanages them; everything has to be done her way. I know how they feel. Jennifer gets very jealous of me spending time with the lads. I used to go out with them on Fridays, but it caused arguments each time, so I stopped. Her son Bobby has started dating a lovely girl. Jennifer is nice to the girl’s face, but when she’s gone, Jennifer picks holes in her. I’ve told her that she can be selfish sometimes. She says she knows; her own mother used to say the same. She says she doesn’t want to be selfish and will try harder. I’ve told her that micromanaging people drives them away - she knew I was talking about more than the supermarket staff.

Jennifer’s Background: Her parents split when Jennifer was 11 years old, she was the oldest child of 4 siblings. Her father said he loved her very much and would still see her every weekend - but soon he just dissolved out of her life. Jennifer started secondary school aged 12. Her best friend from primary school was in her class. When her friend started to make new friends, Jennifer got so angry with her. It wasn’t long before they weren’t speaking. They never made up.

Her brothers and sisters were always quite ’care-free’, but Jennifer was an anxious teenager. She didn’t sleep well at night, and seemed on edge if her mum or siblings were gone for a long time. Her mother started to date another man, Jennifer made it clear that she didn’t want this man in the home even though she couldn’t point to anything wrong with him. Her mum told her off for not caring about anyone’s happiness but her own. As her siblings got older, Jennifer didn’t like sharing her stuff with them. Her mum and siblings said she was getting more and more selfish. Her mum would insist she shared, or take the stuff off her when she refused.

She worked hard at school and wanted a successful career. At university she started dating. Her boyfriend was charming, got her pregnant, and then left her. She raised her son Bobby alone and started working part time in the local supermarket. She taught him to ’work hard’ and ’tell the truth’. She often told him that people who lie are worthless. At 30 she married Glen. He’s a good husband and step-father.
