elements.text:
This study, and the next two, focus on three fears that repeatedly arise in our situations as fallen, finite, and free creatures of God:

  • Am I safe?
  • Am I valuable?
  • Do I belong?
We will look at them in turn.

We feel safe with others when three factors come together:

  • (i) sacrifice - the other person cares for me and will put me first;
  • (ii) competence - they are strong and skilled enough to protect me; and
  • (iii) connection - they understand me and know what I need.

elements.passageText: <sup>6</sup> For while we were still helpless, at the right time Christ died for the ungodly. <sup>7</sup> (For rarely will anyone die for a righteous person, though for a good person perhaps someone might possibly dare to die.) <sup>8</sup> But God demonstrates his own love for us, in that while we were still sinners, Christ died for us.

elements.question: Why can we be confident we are safe with God?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: Paul says Christ died for us "while we were still helpless" and "still sinners" — not after we cleaned ourselves up or proved ourselves trustworthy. The passage notes that rarely would anyone die even for a "righteous" or "good" person, yet God's love went further than human loyalty ever does: Christ died for the ungodly. If God secured our safety with him at our very worst, when we had nothing to offer and no claim on his help, that safety was never earned in the first place, so it can't be lost by falling short again later. It rests on his character, "demonstrated" at the cross, not on our performance.
elements.questionHint: The passage stresses timing — "while we were still helpless... still sinners." Why would God choose to secure our safety at the worst possible moment, rather than waiting until we deserved it?

elements.passageText: <sup>1</sup> God is our strong refuge; he is truly our helper in times of trouble. <sup>2</sup> For this reason we do not fear when the earth shakes, and the mountains tumble into the depths of the sea, <sup>3</sup> when its waves crash and foam, and the mountains shake before the surging sea.

elements.question: Why else can we be confident we are safe with God?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: The psalm calls God "our strong refuge" and "our helper in times of trouble" — not a distant observer but present help precisely when things go wrong. What's striking is the scale of the security this buys: even if the earth itself shakes and mountains topple into the sea, "we do not fear." The psalm isn't promising that nothing bad will happen; it's promising that when the very ground under our feet gives way, God himself doesn't. Our safety was never actually resting on stable circumstances — it rests on him, so it holds even when everything visible is falling apart around us.
elements.questionHint: Notice what's shaking in verses 2-3 — the earth, the mountains, the sea. Why does the psalm reach for the most catastrophic images it can find to describe what our safety in God can survive?

elements.passageText: For we do not have a high priest incapable of sympathizing with our weaknesses, but one who has been tempted in every way just as we are, yet without sin. <sup>16</sup> Therefore let us confidently approach the throne of grace to receive mercy and find grace whenever we need help.

elements.question: Why else can we be confident we are safe with God?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: The writer says our high priest is not "incapable of sympathizing with our weaknesses" because he was "tempted in every way just as we are, yet without sin." That combination matters — he knows temptation and weakness from the inside, so he isn't judging us from a distance, but he also never failed, so he isn't compromised himself. Because of who he is, we can "confidently approach the throne of grace" — not creep in nervously hoping to be tolerated, but come boldly expecting "mercy" and "grace." Our safety with God isn't about avoiding him when we're weak; it's about running toward him, since he already understands.
elements.questionHint: The passage pairs two things about Jesus — he was tempted "just as we are," yet "without sin." How does having both of those together, rather than just one, change how boldly you can approach him?

elements.passageText: <sup>23</sup> “ Look! The virgin will conceive and bear a son, and they will call him Emmanuel,” which means “ God with us .”

elements.question: Why else can we be confident we are safe with God?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: The name given here is "Emmanuel," and Matthew makes sure we don't miss the meaning by translating it for us: "God with us." That's the whole basis for safety in this one verse — not that God watches from heaven or intervenes occasionally, but that in Jesus he actually came and stayed present with humanity. A name like this, given at his birth, sets the direction for everything that follows: wherever else Jesus goes, he is, by definition, God being with us. Safety, here, isn't first a promise about protection from harm so much as a promise that we are never left alone with whatever comes.
elements.questionHint: Matthew doesn't just give the name "Emmanuel" — he stops to translate it for you. Why might he think that meaning, "God with us," is the important thing to notice here?

elements.text:
The opposite is also true when it comes to feeling unsafe. I will feel unsafe to entrust myself to a given person if they are selfish (lack of sacrifice), or if they are weak (lack of competence), or if they don’t ’get’ me (lack of connection - a significant issue for teenagers). If they lack any of these factors, anxiety is likely to return in the form of these questions:

  • Am I going to be hurt? (lack of safety)
  • Am I going to be shamed? (lack of value)
  • Am I going to be left? (lack of belonging)

elements.passageText: <sup>10</sup> There was a famine in the land, so Abram went down to Egypt to stay for a while because the famine was severe. <sup>11</sup> As he approached Egypt, he said to his wife Sarai, “Look, I know that you are a beautiful woman. <sup>12</sup> When the Egyptians see you they will say, ‘This is his wife.’ Then they will kill me but will keep you alive. <sup>13</sup> So tell them you are my sister so that it may go well for me because of you and my life will be spared on account of you.”

elements.question: How does fear over safety lead people astray in this passage?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: Abram is afraid the Egyptians will "kill me but... keep you alive" because of Sarai's beauty, so he tells her to lie and say she's his sister, hoping "it may go well for me" and "my life will be spared." Fear over his own safety leads him to deceive, and to put his wife at risk in a foreign household to protect himself. Rather than trusting the God who had just promised to bless him and make him a great nation, Abram takes matters into his own hands the moment he feels unsafe, and his solution is self-protective at someone else's expense.
elements.questionHint: Look at whose safety Abram is actually protecting with this plan, and whose safety he's willing to risk instead. What does that trade-off show about where his trust really is?

elements.passageText: But the men who had gone up with him said, “We are not able to go up against these people, because they are stronger than we are!” 32 Then they presented the Israelites with a discouraging report of the land they had investigated, saying, “The land that we passed through to investigate is a land that devours its inhabitants. All the people we saw there are of great stature. 33 We even saw the Nephilim there (the descendants of Anak came from the Nephilim), and we seemed liked grasshoppers both to ourselves and to them.” 1 Then all the community raised a loud cry, and the people wept that night. 2 And all the Israelites murmured against Moses and Aaron, and the whole congregation said to them, “If only we had died in the land of Egypt, or if only we had perished in this wilderness! 3 Why has the Lord brought us into this land only to be killed by the sword, that our wives and our children should become plunder? Wouldn’t it be better for us to return to Egypt?” 4 So they said to one another, “Let’s appoint a leader and return to Egypt.”

elements.question: How does fear over safety lead people astray in this passage?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: The spies' report that the land's people are "of great stature" and that they themselves "seemed like grasshoppers" turns the whole community's fear into open rebellion. Instead of trusting the God who had already brought them out of Egypt, the people weep, murmur against Moses and Aaron, and conclude it would be "better for us to return to Egypt" — trading the promise for the safety of the slavery they already knew. Fear doesn't just make them anxious here; it makes them ready to appoint a new leader and reverse the whole journey God had them on, all to avoid a danger they hadn't even faced yet.
elements.questionHint: The people say it would be "better... to return to Egypt" — back to slavery. What does choosing known captivity over an unknown promise reveal about what fear does to their judgment?

elements.passageText: <sup>11</sup> But Samuel said, “What have you done?” Saul replied, “When I saw that the army had started to abandon me and that you didn’t come at the appointed time and that the Philistines had assembled at Micmash, <sup>12</sup> I thought, ‘Now the Philistines will come down on me at Gilgal and I have not sought the Lord’s favor.’ So I felt obligated to offer the burnt offering.” <sup>13</sup> Then Samuel said to Saul, “You have made a foolish choice! You have not obeyed the commandment that the Lord your God gave you. Had you done that, the Lord would have established your kingdom over Israel forever! <sup>14</sup> But now your kingdom will not continue! The Lord has sought out for himself a man who is loyal to him and the Lord has appointed him to be leader over his people, for you have not obeyed what the Lord commanded you.” ... <sup>24</sup> Then Saul said to Samuel, “I have sinned, for I have disobeyed what the Lord commanded and what you said as well. For I was afraid of the army, and I followed their wishes.

elements.question: How does fear over safety lead people astray in this passage?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: Saul explains himself by saying he saw "the army had started to abandon me" and panicked, so he "felt obligated" to offer the sacrifice himself rather than wait for Samuel — and later admits plainly, "I was afraid of the army, and I followed their wishes." In both moments, fear of losing his men's confidence pushes Saul to disobey a direct command from God, first by overstepping his role, then by giving in to pressure. Samuel calls it a "foolish choice" that costs him the kingdom. Fear of what people would do led Saul to care more about appearing in control than about obedience.
elements.questionHint: Saul says he acted because he saw the army starting to leave him, and later that he "followed their wishes." Whose approval was he really afraid of losing — God's, or the army's?

elements.passageText: <sup>3</sup> Elijah was afraid, so he got up and fled for his life to Beer Sheba in Judah. He left his servant there, <sup>4</sup> while he went a day’s journey into the desert. He went and sat down under a shrub and asked the Lord to take his life: “I’ve had enough! Now, O Lord , take my life. After all, I’m no better than my ancestors.”

elements.question: How does fear over safety lead people astray in this passage?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: Elijah, fresh off a massive victory over the prophets of Baal, hears one threat from Jezebel and is "afraid," so he flees "for his life" all the way to the desert, where he asks God to let him die: "I've had enough... take my life." Fear here doesn't just make him run from danger — it collapses him into despair, convincing him he's "no better than" his ancestors and that giving up is the only option left. Real fear over safety can swing all the way from fight to total collapse, making someone want to escape not just the threat but life itself.
elements.questionHint: Elijah runs to save his life, then immediately asks God to take it. What does that contradiction tell you about what fear had actually done to him, beyond just wanting to escape Jezebel?

elements.passageText: <sup>69</sup> Now Peter was sitting outside in the courtyard. A slave girl came to him and said, “You also were with Jesus the Galilean.” <sup>70</sup> But he denied it in front of them all: “I don’t know what you’re talking about!” <sup>71</sup> When he went out to the gateway, another slave girl saw him and said to the people there, “This man was with Jesus the Nazarene.” <sup>72</sup> He denied it again with an oath, “I do not know the man!” <sup>73</sup> After a little while, those standing there came up to Peter and said, “You really are one of them too – even your accent gives you away!” <sup>74</sup> At that he began to curse, and he swore with an oath, “I do not know the man!” At that moment a rooster crowed.

elements.question: How does fear over safety lead people astray in this passage?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: Three times Peter is recognized as one of Jesus' followers, and three times fear for his own safety leads him further into denial — first a plain "I don't know what you're talking about," then a denial "with an oath," and finally he "began to curse" and swear he doesn't know "the man." Each accusation escalates his fear and each response escalates his betrayal, until he's cursing to distance himself from the very person he'd sworn loyalty to hours earlier. Fear over safety doesn't stay contained here — it compounds, pulling Peter further from Jesus with each repetition until the rooster's crow exposes exactly how far he's gone.
elements.questionHint: Notice how Peter's denials escalate each time — from a plain statement to an oath to cursing. What does that escalation show about what fear does the longer it's given room to grow?

elements.text:
Just as many dangerous lies contain a semblance of truth, so many dangerous relationships contain a semblance of safety. Here are some examples of corrupt, counterfeit, and/or exploitative versions of safety:

  • Prison: Security comes at the cost of freedom.
  • Parenting: parents should provide children with a safe zone, but sometimes this can drift towards becoming something like a prison (due to a lack of freedom). We need to remember that, in time, such prisons will be broken out of.
  • Political security: The desire for national security (perhaps in the face of terrorist threats) can be used as a reason to sacrifice freedom.
  • Job security: the desire for financial security can hold you hostage in a job that you might be wiser to move on from.
  • Controlling relationships: Some romantic partners will seem to offer security, but again at the cost of freedom.

elements.passageText: <sup>3</sup> Do not trust in princes, or in human beings, who cannot deliver!<sup>4</sup> Their life’s breath departs, they return to the ground; on that day their plans die.

elements.question: Why is it bad to trust for safety in the wrong place?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: The psalm's reasoning is blunt: don't trust in princes or people because they "cannot deliver" — and then it explains why not: their "life's breath departs, they return to the ground," and on that day even their plans "die" along with them. Human protectors are limited by their own mortality; whatever security they offer only lasts as long as they do, and then it's gone along with every intention they had to help you. Trusting for safety in the wrong place here specifically means trusting something with an expiration date built into it — building your sense of security on a foundation that will eventually fail simply because it will die.
elements.questionHint: The psalm's reason for not trusting in "princes" isn't that they're untrustworthy people — it's that "their life's breath departs." What kind of limitation is that, and why does it apply to every human protector eventually?

4 So all the elders of Israel gathered together and approached Samuel at Ramah. 5 They said to him, “Look, you are old, and your sons don’t follow your ways. So now appoint over us a king to lead us, just like all the other nations have.”

For it is not you that they have rejected, but it is me that they have rejected as their king. 8 Just as they have done from the day that I brought them up from Egypt until this very day, they have rejected me and have served other gods. 19 But the people refused to heed Samuel’s warning. Instead they said, “No! There will be a king over us!

elements.question: Why else is it bad to trust for safety in the wrong place?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: Israel demands a king "to lead us, just like all the other nations have," and God tells Samuel plainly that in doing so "it is me that they have rejected as their king." The passage then spells out exactly what this trade will cost: the king will take their sons, daughters, fields, and servants, and a tenth of everything they own, until "you yourselves will be his servants." Seeking safety in a human king instead of God isn't neutral here — it means swapping a relationship with God as protector for submission to a ruler who will eventually take from them the very things they were trying to secure.
elements.questionHint: God says that in asking for a king, the people have rejected him specifically "as their king." What does it mean that wanting a different kind of protector is really a rejection of God in that particular role?

elements.passageText: <sup>13</sup> “Do so because my people have committed a double wrong: they have rejected me, the fountain of life-giving water, and they have dug cisterns for themselves, cracked cisterns which cannot even hold water.”

elements.question: Why else is it bad to trust for safety in the wrong place?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: God names the "double wrong" precisely: his people have "rejected me, the fountain of life-giving water," and instead "dug cisterns for themselves" — cisterns that are "cracked" and "cannot even hold water." The image is almost absurd: they abandoned a constantly flowing spring for containers they built themselves that leak everything out. Trusting the wrong source for safety isn't just risky here, it's self-defeating — the substitute doesn't merely provide less than God does, it actively fails to hold what little it's given, leaving people thirsty by their own effort after walking away from the one supply that never runs dry.
elements.questionHint: Look closely at the two water sources being compared — a "fountain of life-giving water" versus cisterns that are "cracked." What's the difference between a source that flows and one that has to hold what it's given?

elements.passageText: <sup>19</sup> “Do not accumulate for yourselves treasures on earth, where moth and rust destroy and where thieves break in and steal. <sup>20</sup> But accumulate for yourselves treasures in heaven, where moth and rust do not destroy, and thieves do not break in and steal. <sup>21</sup> For where your treasure is, there your heart will be also.

elements.question: Why else is it bad to trust for safety in the wrong place?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: Jesus points out that earthly treasure is vulnerable in ways heavenly treasure isn't: "moth and rust destroy" it, and "thieves break in and steal" it — decay and theft both apply. Anything stored up here is only ever temporarily yours, subject to forces you can't fully control. Then comes the real reason this matters: "where your treasure is, there your heart will be also." It's not just that earthly security can be lost; it's that wherever you park your trust for safekeeping is where your heart ends up living, so trusting the wrong place doesn't just risk your stuff, it relocates your heart to something that can't last.
elements.questionHint: Jesus doesn't just say earthly treasure can be lost — he adds "where your treasure is, there your heart will be also." What does that connect your sense of safety to, beyond just your possessions?

elements.passageText: <sup>17</sup> Command those who are rich in this world’s goods not to be haughty or to set their hope on riches, which are uncertain, but on God who richly provides us with all things for our enjoyment.

elements.question: What should we do instead, and why?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: Paul's instruction is direct: don't "set your hope on riches, which are uncertain," but set it "on God who richly provides us with all things for our enjoyment." The contrast is between two objects of hope, one described as inherently unstable ("uncertain") and the other described by his generous, reliable character — he's the one who "richly provides." Notice, too, that the alternative isn't grim self-denial; God is the one who gives good things "for our enjoyment." The answer to insecurity isn't to stop wanting good things, but to relocate your hope from an unreliable pile of resources onto the reliable giver behind every resource you have.
elements.questionHint: Paul contrasts riches, which are "uncertain," with God, who "richly provides." What's the difference between hoping in a pile of resources and hoping in the generous person who keeps supplying them?

elements.question: Help Jennifer Feel Safe ...
elements.answer:
Mistake: It is likely a mistake to rebuke Jennifer for selfishness, to call her to sacrificial giving, or to stop being ’me’ focused, to care for others.

Gospel Angle: Jennifer’s key problem is that she doesn’t feel safe, and so she cannot (or will not) entrust herself to others. The way she sees life, people take from her, and people leave. She needs to hear of the God who has pursued her, her whole life, and who sees her as precious. The Father who sees her brokenness, sin and shortcoming, and who loves her still! The Son who gave up everything to become human and die for her. The Good Shepherd who walks with her and will never leave her, who loved her so much he laid down his life for her to bring her forgiveness.

She seems selfish because she grips everything in a tight fist. We can rebuke her and tell her to open the fist; we can try to pull things out of her clenched fist; or we can show her she is safe. If we show her she is safe - and if she accepts that truth - then one day, her hand will open wide.

Think of how to gain the trust of an abused dog - you don’t scold it; you sit with it and share your food with it. You show it that you are safe.

For her Pastor: Jennifer’s situation cannot be rushed. Words are cheap to her - she has trusted people and their words in the past, and they let her down. She feels shame about her selfishness, so rather than rebuke her further, empathise and show that we all struggle. Praise her for how she has raised Bobby, and encourage her for the strength she has shown to get through her difficulties in life. Remind her that God walks with her. He knows our weakness - the bruised reed he will not break.

For her Church: Resist asking Jennifer to serve. To someone else, this would be a great way to bring them on board and help them feel like they belong. To Jennifer, it just feels like more people are trying to take from her. Find ways for folk in the church to serve her where it’s clear there are no ’strings attached’. If she is unwell, have someone drop round food.

For her friends & family - Glen: Glen should keep reassuring her that he loves her and is here to stay. He could treat her to the beauty salon with his money, praise her for the times she looks out for others, or tell her how much he appreciates it when she shows kindness to him or others.

For her friends & family - Bobby: Bobby should assure her that no-one could ever replace her as his Mum. His girlfriend is different, she is not a threat or a rival to Jennifer. He wants to one day be the husband for a lady that his dad never was to Jennifer - Jennifer has raised him that way.

elements.text: We are intrinsically valuable, because God has made us so.

elements.passageText: <sup>27</sup>  God created humankind in his own image, in the image of God he created them, male and female he created them.

elements.question: Why can we be confident we are valued by God?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: The verse repeats itself for emphasis — "God created humankind in his own image, in the image of God he created them" — as if to make sure the point isn't missed: every human being, "male and female," bears the very image of God. This isn't a value earned by achievement or granted by other people's opinions; it's built into what a human being is from the moment of creation. Because the image comes from being made by God rather than from anything we've done, it belongs equally to every person and can't be added to or taken away by circumstance — our value is a fact about our origin, not a verdict on our performance.
elements.questionHint: The verse says "in his own image" twice in one sentence. Why might it repeat that phrase instead of just saying it once?

elements.passageText: <sup>8</sup> But God demonstrates his own love for us, in that while we were still sinners, Christ died for us. ...  <sup>10</sup>For if while we were enemies we were reconciled to God through the death of his Son, how much more, since we have been reconciled, will we be saved by his life?

elements.question: Why can we be confident we are valued by God?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: Paul says God "demonstrates his own love for us" specifically through the fact that "while we were still sinners, Christ died for us" — the value God places on us isn't a response to our goodness, since there wasn't any; it's proven at the exact moment we least deserved it. Then he pushes further: if being "enemies" of God still got us reconciled through Christ's death, "how much more" can we expect from an ongoing relationship with him now, "since we have been reconciled." The logic moves from the hardest case to the easier one — if he valued us enough to die for us as enemies, our worth to him now, as reconciled children, is even more secure.
elements.questionHint: Paul argues from the harder case to the easier one — "if... enemies... how much more" now that we're reconciled. Why does starting with the "hardest" version of the argument make the conclusion more certain, not less?

elements.passageText: <sup>26</sup> For in Christ Jesus you are all sons of God through faith. <sup>27</sup> For all of you who were baptized into Christ have clothed yourselves with Christ. <sup>28</sup> There is neither Jew nor Greek, there is neither slave nor free, there is neither male nor female – for all of you are one in Christ Jesus. <sup>29</sup> And if you belong to Christ, then you are Abraham’s descendants, heirs according to the promise.

elements.question: Why can we be confident we are valued by God?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: Paul says that "through faith" in Christ, believers have "clothed yourselves with Christ," and this erases the categories that usually divide people's worth from each other — "neither Jew nor Greek... neither slave nor free... neither male nor female," because "all of you are one in Christ Jesus." Whatever hierarchy of value the world assigns based on ethnicity, social status, or gender, Paul says it doesn't apply inside this identity. And the value isn't abstract — being "in Christ" makes you "Abraham's descendants, heirs according to the promise," meaning you inherit everything that promise carries. Our value here comes from union with Christ, not from any category the world ranks people by.
elements.questionHint: Paul lists three pairs the world usually ranks — Jew/Greek, slave/free, male/female — and says none of them apply. What does "all of you are one in Christ Jesus" replace those rankings with?

elements.text: God has given each of us an amazing set of gifts. That means we each have something to offer this world, an ability to make a difference. We often say that comparing ourselves to others is a bad idea (“comparison is the thief of joy”) and often it is, because we do it in a bad way. But there is a humble and grateful way that we can compare ourselves with others, so as to figure out how God has gifted us specifically.

elements.passageText: <sup>12</sup> For just as the body is one and yet has many members, and all the members of the body – though many – are one body, so too is Christ. <sup>13</sup> For in one Spirit we were all baptized into one body. Whether Jews or Greeks or slaves or free, we were all made to drink of the one Spirit. <sup>14</sup> For in fact the body is not a single member, but many. <sup>15</sup> If the foot says, “Since I am not a hand, I am not part of the body,” it does not lose its membership in the body because of that. <sup>16</sup> And if the ear says, “Since I am not an eye, I am not part of the body,” it does not lose its membership in the body because of that. <sup>17</sup> If the whole body were an eye, what part would do the hearing? If the whole were an ear, what part would exercise the sense of smell? <sup>18</sup> But as a matter of fact, God has placed each of the members in the body just as he decided. <sup>19</sup> If they were all the same member, where would the body be? <sup>20</sup> So now there are many members, but one body.

elements.question: Why can we be confident our gifts matter?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: Paul insists that a foot which says "I am not part of the body" because it isn't a hand "does not lose its membership in the body because of that" — its value isn't determined by resembling the more prominent parts. He drives the logic home with the eye and the ear: if the whole body were just one part, "what part would do the hearing" or exercise smell? Diversity of function is the point, not a flaw — "God has placed each of the members in the body just as he decided." Your gift matters not because it's the flashiest one, but because God deliberately placed it there, and the body needs exactly that function to work at all.
elements.questionHint: Paul asks what would happen if the whole body were just one part, like an eye. What does that question reveal about why God "placed each of the members... just as he decided" instead of making them all the same?

elements.text: What are the gifts that God has given you, that he hasn’t given to everyone? How can you serve God well, as the person you are, with the gifts you have been given? Paying attention to our value as represented in the specific giftedness with which God has blessed us is not (necessarily) prideful. It can be done in a spirit of thankfulness.

elements.passageText: <sup>13</sup> Certainly you made my mind and heart; you wove me together in my mother’s womb. <sup>14</sup> I will give you thanks because your deeds are awesome and amazing. You knew me thoroughly; <sup>15</sup> my bones were not hidden from you, when I was made in secret and sewed together in the depths of the earth.

elements.question: Are you just generically special or a precious ’one-off’ (& why)?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: The psalmist says God "wove" him together in his mother's womb — a craftsman's word, describing individual, hands-on work rather than mass production — and responds not with generic gratitude but personal amazement: "your deeds are awesome and amazing... you knew me thoroughly." That last phrase is key: this isn't God knowing humanity as a category, but knowing this one person completely and specifically. Being "special" in a general sense would mean sharing a label with everyone else; being individually woven and thoroughly known is different — it means God's attention and craftsmanship were personally directed at you, not distributed generically across the species.
elements.questionHint: The psalmist doesn't just say God made him — he says God "wove" him together and "knew me thoroughly." What's the difference between being made as part of a general category and being individually woven and thoroughly known?

elements.text:
The significant people in the community around us - our family and friends, our colleagues and community leaders - can also help build up our understanding of our value when they tell us of that value, and even, simply, when they pay attention to us.

Feelings of being valueless come about if we allow ourselves to believe lies. These might be lies that we push onto ourselves, or others may try to push them onto us. They include statements like: ‘I’m no good at anything’ or ’I’m worthless’ or ’Nobody could love me’ or ’I do everything wrong.’ We must reject these lies.

elements.passageText: <sup>5</sup> They do all their deeds to be seen by people, for they make their phylacteries wide and their tassels long. <sup>6</sup> They love the place of honor at banquets and the best seats in the synagogues <sup>7</sup> and elaborate greetings in the marketplaces, and to have people call them ‘Rabbi.’

elements.question: How does seeking value in the wrong place lead people astray?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: Jesus describes people who do "all their deeds to be seen by people" — even religious practices like wide phylacteries and long tassels become props for an audience rather than genuine devotion. They chase "the place of honor at banquets," "the best seats in the synagogues," "elaborate greetings," and being called "Rabbi." Every item on this list is about being noticed and honored by others, listed almost as a catalogue of hollow substitutes. Seeking value this way turns worship, hospitality, and titles into performances calculated for applause, so the person ends up defined by how impressively they can be seen rather than by anything real underneath the display.
elements.questionHint: Look at the specific things this list obsesses over — wide phylacteries, best seats, being called "Rabbi." What do all of these have in common as ways of getting value from other people rather than from God?

elements.passageText: <sup>5</sup> “Whenever you pray, do not be like the hypocrites, because they love to pray while standing in synagogues and on street corners so that people can see them. Truly I say to you, they have their reward.

elements.question: How else does seeking value in the wrong place lead people astray?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: Jesus singles out people who "love to pray... on street corners so that people can see them," and his verdict is almost clinical: "they have their reward." The prayer accomplishes exactly what they were actually after — being seen — so there's nothing more coming from God for it. The problem isn't public prayer itself but the motive behind choosing street corners: it's staged for an audience, not directed to God. Seeking value this way is self-limiting; you get precisely the human attention you were angling for, and that's the whole payout, because you were never actually addressing the one who could give you anything more.
elements.questionHint: Jesus says people who pray to be seen "have their reward." If the reward is simply being seen by people, what does that mean is missing from the transaction — what didn't they get?

elements.text: Dangerous relationships offer us a semblance of value without the reality. Flattery offers us attention at the cost of genuineness. The flatterer seems to affirm our value in their eyes, but without caring about what they really say. The ’value’ offered to us is superficial. Many young people are exploited by romantic partners smart enough to tell them what they want to hear, especially if the young person grew up in situations where they did not feel valued.

elements.passageText: <sup>44</sup> How can you believe, if you accept praise from one another and don’t seek the praise that comes from the only God?

elements.question: Why is it bad to seek value and affirmation in the wrong place?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: Jesus asks how it's even possible to believe while "you accept praise from one another and don't seek the praise that comes from the only God" — the two pursuits are framed as functionally incompatible. Chasing human approval and seeking God's approval aren't just different priorities; wanting one badly enough can crowd out the capacity for faith itself, since believing in Jesus often means accepting what God says over what people around you are applauding. Seeking value from human praise is bad here not just because it's shallow, but because it can actually block the very belief that would connect you to the praise that matters — God's own verdict on you.
elements.questionHint: Jesus doesn't just say seeking human praise is inferior — he asks how you "can believe" while doing it. What does that suggest human praise-seeking actually competes with or crowds out?

elements.passageText: <sup>23</sup> Whatever you are doing, work at it with enthusiasm, as to the Lord and not for people, <sup>24</sup> because you know that you will receive your inheritance from the Lord as the reward. Serve the Lord Christ.

elements.question: What is the alternative?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: Paul's alternative is to work "as to the Lord and not for people," whatever the task is — "whatever you are doing." That single shift in audience changes everything: the same work, done for the same people, in the same job, is redirected toward God as the one you're actually serving and pleasing. And the payoff matches — "you will receive your inheritance from the Lord as the reward," not merely a paycheck or applause from a boss. Instead of seeking value through others' recognition, you work "with enthusiasm" because your worth and your reward are already settled by Christ, whom Paul says plainly you are actually serving.
elements.questionHint: Paul says to work "as to the Lord and not for people." What changes about your motivation and reward when you picture the one you're ultimately working for as Christ rather than whoever happens to be watching?

elements.text: Evangelicals are good at explaining sin - and at telling people they are sinful. Evangelicals are not always so good at telling people they are precious. We are glorious ruins - we are broken, beautiful beings. God created us for glory, and despite our fallenness, he has set his love on us. He has forgiven our sin, and he has chosen to delight in us.

elements.passageText: <sup>17</sup> The Lord your God is in your midst; he is a warrior who can deliver. He takes great delight in you; he renews you by his love; he shouts for joy over you.

elements.question: How would you respond to someone who says that God forgives us and then just patiently endures our failings?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: This verse doesn't describe patient endurance at all — it describes delight. God "takes great delight in you," "renews you by his love," and even "shouts for joy" over his people. Someone merely tolerating another person's failings doesn't sing over them; they put up with them quietly, maybe with a sigh. But the picture here is active, joyful, even loud — closer to a parent thrilled with a child than a landlord tolerating a difficult tenant. If this is accurate, then forgiveness isn't God gritting his teeth and waiting us out; it's paired with him being genuinely glad to be near us, delighting rather than merely enduring.
elements.questionHint: The passage uses the words "delight" and "shouts for joy." How is joyfully shouting over someone different from patiently putting up with them?

elements.question: Help George know he’s valued ...
elements.answer:
Mistake: In this situation, further ’tough love’ is unlikely to help George.

Gospel Angle: George needs to hear that he is special and unique, woven together in his mother’s womb. He needs to know that God loved him so much Christ died for him to forgive his sins. He needs to believe that God has seen George in his weakest most vulnerable state and yet God delights in him. There is no shame with God, he has cleansed us from our sins, we are clothed in Christ’s righteousness and beauty. God sees George exactly as he is - and God loves him. God has given each of us gifts. He has given George a unique set of gifts to bring blessing to those around him. He needs to know that ’ears aren’t blind.’ That’s the wrong way to look at people: ‘ears are designed to hear’. He needs to see that he has a purpose in this world, and to discover who God has designed him to be (and it’s not a farmer!), so that he can make a difference in this world to the glory of God.

For his Pastor: George needs someone to believe in him. Someone to help him explore who he is. His whole life, authority figures have told him he is a ’blind ear.’ There is a danger that, in the short term, an authority figure who shows George respect could be confusing for him, and sexual attraction could kick in. The pastor needs to avoid situations that could add to this interpretation, and also needs to not panic if there are signs of it.

For his Church: Give opportunities for George to explore and develop his gifts. Find an older man to mentor him, one who can encourage him and help him explore his gifts. In time, teach George how he himself can become a mentor to younger men. In time, we want George to be able to see that he wasn’t pathetic as a boy, he just needed a compassionate authority figure to help him figure out who he was. Maybe George can be part of helping this be done for other young men, and maybe he can let Jesus do it for him.

For his Family & Friends: It is a tough call with family. It would be amazing if George’s father could appreciate who his son is, and not who he wants him to be. That is worth trying for, but it is also worth knowing in advance that it might be a hard perspective for George’s father to embrace. Much the same is true for his brothers also. As to the issue of living at home - if there is no progress, George might need to be encouraged to take the next step of independence and move out. But some confidence building might need to happen first.

In terms of safety, value, and belonging, George needs help with all three: he needs to feel safe, he needs to feel he is valued, and he needs to belong. Most especially, perhaps, he needs to feel valued. It is also important that he comes to know safety, value and belonging both vertically (with God) and horizontally (with other people). He needs to base his primary sense of safety, value, and belonging on the vertical (God), but he also needs support with the horizontal (from his pastor, his church, and - ideally - his family and friends).

elements.question: married, late 30s
elements.answer:
Stanley is a farmer, he has been married for 12 years and has three children. His wife, Debbie, is pursuing divorce, she began the process a couple of years ago but Stanley talked her out of it. She thought he might change but he hasn’t and she is set on leaving him. Debbie says that Stanley is married to the farm, he is never in the house, they don’t go on dates, they don’t go on holiday together, he doesn’t spend any time with the kids unless they are working with him. Stanley says he is doing his best to provide for his family and do an honest day’s work. He knows he should spend more time with his wife and kids and he desperately doesn’t want to lose them, but every time they have an argument about it, he makes an effort to be present in the home but it soon fades away. Debbie has had enough.

Stanley’s Background

  • Stanley was brought up in a loving Christian home as a child. He loves and respects his father & mother. His Dad often pops down to the farm to give him a hand and Stanley loves spending time with him working.
  • He doesn’t go to church much and struggles to respect the local minister of the church. He says, ‘It’s hard to listen to someone who hasn’t done a hard day’s work in his life.’
  • Stanley gets on well with his oldest son, who is a natural farmer and loves the work. The middle son and Stanley don’t get on so well. The middle son would rather meet up with his friends on a Saturday than join in with the farm work. Sometimes Stanley can belittle him for being lazy.
  • Stanley loves his father and looks up to him. When Stanley was 11, he was riding in the tractor with his Dad and on the road they got stuck behind traffic going to the local football match, some flashy BMW cars were in front of them and he saw his father get visibly agitated. His father said to Stanley: ‘Look at those wasters. They drive around enjoying themselves, spending their days watching football, probably living off the government, or their rich parents. It’s people like that that are destroying our country, they couldn’t do a day’s work if their life depended on it. They make me sick.’

elements.text: We all want to belong, and ultimately, we belong to God.

elements.passageText: <sup>7</sup> I will take you to myself for a people, and I will be your God. Then you will know that I am the Lord your God, who brought you out from your enslavement to the Egyptians.

elements.question: Why can we be confident we belong to and with God?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: God's promise is mutual and personal: "I will take you to myself for a people, and I will be your God." He doesn't just offer protection or blessing from a distance — he claims Israel as his own and commits himself to them in return, a two-way belonging. And this claim is grounded in what he's already done: "who brought you out from your enslavement to the Egyptians." The belonging isn't a future hope to hope for; it's anchored in a rescue that already happened. Because God himself initiates and secures the relationship — "I will take you... I will be" — our belonging to him rests on his action, not on our holding up our end.
elements.questionHint: God says "I will take you to myself" and "I will be your God" — both actions are his, not ours. What does it mean that he's the one securing the belonging rather than leaving it up to us to earn or maintain?

elements.passageText: <sup>22</sup> Then you will again be my people and I will be your God.

elements.question: Why else can we be confident we belong to and with God?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: This short promise comes after a long section of judgment and exile, yet God still says, "you will again be my people and I will be your God." Even after failure serious enough to bring discipline, the relationship isn't permanently severed — it's restored, stated in exactly the same mutual terms as before: his people, their God. The word "again" matters here; it acknowledges the belonging was broken or strained, and promises it will be renewed all the same. Belonging to God, in other words, survives even seasons where it looked lost, because it depends on his commitment to restore it, not on an unbroken record from us.
elements.questionHint: The verse says "again" — implying the relationship had been interrupted. What does it mean for belonging that God promises to restore it rather than treating the break as final?

elements.passageText: <sup>13</sup> And when you heard the word of truth (the gospel of your salvation) – when you believed in Christ – you were marked with the seal of the promised Holy Spirit, <sup>14</sup> who is the down payment of our inheritance, until the redemption of God’s own possession, to the praise of his glory.

elements.question: Why else can we be confident we belong to and with God?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: Paul describes believers as "marked with the seal of the promised Holy Spirit" the moment they believed the gospel — a seal being a mark of ownership and authenticity, not something casual or easily erased. And the Spirit isn't just decorative; he's "the down payment of our inheritance," a guarantee that more is coming, "until the redemption of God's own possession." Notice that last phrase — God's own possession. Belonging here isn't vague sentiment; it's described with the language of a legal seal and a financial down payment, both concrete guarantees that what's begun will be completed and that we are, specifically, his.
elements.questionHint: Paul uses two very concrete images — a "seal" and a "down payment." What do those two words, taken from ownership and finance, guarantee about whether this belonging will hold?

elements.passageText: <sup>16</sup> The Spirit himself bears witness to our spirit that we are God’s children. <sup>17</sup> And if children, then heirs (namely, heirs of God and also fellow heirs with Christ) – if indeed we suffer with him so we may also be glorified with him.

elements.question: Why else can we be confident we belong to and with God?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: Paul says "the Spirit himself bears witness to our spirit that we are God's children" — an inner testimony, not something we have to talk ourselves into or prove by performance. And the passage doesn't stop at the label "children"; it draws out the legal implication — "if children, then heirs," specifically "heirs of God and also fellow heirs with Christ." Belonging to God's family here comes with an actual inheritance attached, shared jointly with Jesus himself. The one condition mentioned, suffering with him so as to also "be glorified with him," suggests this belonging is real enough to walk through hardship alongside Christ, not just a comfortable status held at arm's length.
elements.questionHint: The passage moves from "children" straight to "heirs... fellow heirs with Christ." What does adding the word "heirs" say about what belonging to God's family actually includes, beyond just the relationship itself?

elements.text:
In human relationships, we feel we belong when we know we are part of something bigger than ourselves, when we can recognise meaning and purpose to our role within the community, and when we feel accepted - that it is safe to be seen by others. We feel we belong when we feel at ’home’ with people, when we feel part of a community, when we feel connected to others.

The opposite is also true. If these factors are missing, you won’t feel that you belong. For example, you’ll struggle to belong if you are seen as the ’Black Sheep’ of the family, or if you feel isolated from others or rejected by others, or if you feel you have to hide who you are to blend in, or if you question what your place in this world is.

elements.passageText: <sup>1</sup> Now Jephthah the Gileadite was a brave warrior. His mother was a prostitute, but Gilead was his father. <sup>2</sup> Gilead’s wife also gave him sons. When his wife’s sons grew up, they made Jephthah leave and said to him, “You are not going to inherit any of our father’s wealth, because you are another woman’s son.” <sup>3</sup> So Jephthah left his half-brothers and lived in the land of Tob. Lawless men joined Jephthah’s gang and traveled with him.

elements.question: When Jephthah is rejected, what sort of community does he find?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: Rejected by his half-brothers, who tell him he won't "inherit any of our father's wealth" because he's "another woman's son," Jephthah doesn't find restoration or a new family in any conventional sense — he finds "lawless men" who "joined Jephthah's gang" in the land of Tob. It's belonging, but the only kind available to someone thrown out of legitimate community: an outlaw band formed around shared rejection rather than shared values. The passage is honest about how this works — when people are excluded from the community that should have taken them in, they often end up bound instead to whatever group will have them, however unstable.
elements.questionHint: The text specifically calls the men who join Jephthah "lawless" and describes their group as a "gang." What kind of belonging is this compared to the family inheritance Jephthah was just denied?

elements.text: Dangerous relationships may offer us a semblance of belonging, but without the reality of true belonging. Peer pressure tempts you to belong at the cost of authenticity - succumbing to things that go against your values, in order to belong. Diversity is not celebrated, and you are told (implicitly or explicitly) that you have to conform to a certain standard in order to belong. Authenticity is not valued, and it is not safe to be seen for who you really are.

elements.passageText: <sup>2</sup> Do not be conformed to this present world, but be transformed by the renewing of your mind, so that you may test and approve what is the will of God – what is good and well-pleasing and perfect.

elements.question: What is the alternative to this sort of wrong conformity?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: Paul's alternative to being "conformed to this present world" is being "transformed by the renewing of your mind." Notice the contrast in verbs — conformed is a passive shaping from outside pressure, while transformed describes an inward change that then reorients how you think. The purpose clause matters too: this renewal lets you "test and approve what is the will of God," discovering for yourself that it is "good and well-pleasing and perfect." Instead of belonging defined by matching the world's mold, Paul offers belonging rooted in a mind actually being remade by God, one capable of recognizing and embracing what's genuinely good rather than just going along with the crowd.
elements.questionHint: Paul contrasts being "conformed" to the world with being "transformed" by a renewed mind. What's the difference between a shape pressed onto you from outside and a change that happens from the inside out?

elements.text: Slightly different is the temptation to join the crowd and lose yourself. Going with the flow of the people around you, and abdicating your own responsibility. Another temptation is to find belonging by excluding others. Some groups make their members feel superior by keeping others away. When a fellowship is working well, the mutual love it embodies overflows to draw others in. When a fellowship is not working well, it tries to keep others out. This form of negative fellowship is not based on love, but on power and exclusion.

elements.passageText: <sup>2</sup> “You must not follow a crowd in doing evil things; in a lawsuit you must not offer testimony that agrees with a crowd so as to pervert justice,

elements.question: How does seeking the wrong sort of belonging lead people astray?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: The command is specific and almost surprising in its context — "you must not follow a crowd in doing evil things," including in court, where you must not "offer testimony that agrees with a crowd so as to pervert justice." The danger named here isn't peer pressure in the abstract; it's the very concrete way group consensus can quietly override truth, even in something as serious as legal testimony. Wanting to belong to the crowd's opinion can lead someone to say what everyone else is saying rather than what's actually true, and the passage treats that as an active perversion of justice, not a harmless case of just going along.
elements.questionHint: This command shows up specifically in the context of courtroom testimony. Why might "following a crowd" be especially dangerous when the stakes are telling the truth?

elements.passageText: <sup>24</sup> Then Saul said to Samuel, “I have sinned, for I have disobeyed what the Lord commanded and what you said as well. For I was afraid of the army, and I followed their wishes.

elements.question: How else does seeking the wrong sort of belonging lead people astray?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: Saul's own explanation for his disobedience is telling: "I was afraid of the army, and I followed their wishes." He knew what God and Samuel had commanded, but the pull to stay in step with what his soldiers wanted overrode it. This is belonging gone wrong in a specific way — not seeking approval from strangers, but caving to the group he was supposed to be leading, prioritizing their wishes over God's explicit command. Saul confesses it plainly as sin, which shows the passage isn't excusing him as merely weak; wanting to keep the army's confidence and cohesion led him straight into open disobedience.
elements.questionHint: Saul says he "followed their wishes" instead of God's command. As the king who was supposed to be leading the army, what does it say that he let their wishes lead him instead?

elements.passageText: <sup>11</sup> But when Cephas came to Antioch, I opposed him to his face, because he had clearly done wrong.  <sup>12</sup> Until certain people came from James, he had been eating with the Gentiles. But when they arrived, he stopped doing this and separated himself because he was afraid of those who were pro-circumcision. <sup>13</sup> And the rest of the Jews also joined with him in this hypocrisy, so that even Barnabas was led astray with them by their hypocrisy.

elements.question: How else does seeking the wrong sort of belonging lead people astray?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: Peter had "been eating with the Gentiles" freely, but the moment certain people arrived "from James," he "stopped doing this and separated himself because he was afraid of those who were pro-circumcision." Fear of losing standing with one group led him to abandon a practice he knew was right, and the effect spread — "the rest of the Jews also joined with him in this hypocrisy," pulling in even Barnabas. Paul calls it exactly what it is: hypocrisy. Wanting to belong with the wrong group here didn't just compromise Peter privately; it was contagious, dragging others who respected him into the same inconsistency.
elements.questionHint: Paul notes that even Barnabas, someone respected and mature, "was led astray" by Peter's example. What does that spread show about how one person's fear-driven need to belong can affect a whole community?

elements.passageText: <sup>3</sup> Acknowledge that the Lord is God! He made us and we belong to him; we are his people, the sheep of his pasture.

elements.question: What should we remind ourselves of instead?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: The psalm grounds belonging in a simple fact to "acknowledge": "the Lord is God! He made us and we belong to him." Belonging here isn't something to achieve or negotiate; it's a reality that already exists because of who made us, and the only appropriate response is to recognize it. The image that follows, "we are his people, the sheep of his pasture," adds warmth to the fact — sheep in a shepherd's pasture are cared for and kept close, not merely owned as property. Remembering this shifts belonging from a question we're anxiously trying to answer to a settled fact we simply need to acknowledge.
elements.questionHint: The psalm calls this something to "acknowledge," as if it's already true and just needs recognizing. What's the difference between belonging you have to secure and belonging you just need to remember?

elements.passageText: <sup>1</sup> Now, this is what the Lord says, the one who created you, O Jacob, and formed you, O Israel: “Don’t be afraid, for I will protect you. I call you by name, you are mine.

elements.question: What else should we remind ourselves of instead?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: God speaks here as "the one who created you" and "formed you," and from that identity gives a command and a claim: "Don't be afraid, for I will protect you. I call you by name, you are mine." Being known by name, rather than as part of an anonymous group, is central to the reassurance — this isn't generic ownership but personal, individual claiming. The promise of protection is tied directly to that belonging: because you are his, specifically and by name, fear has less ground to stand on. Remembering this means recalling not just that God exists, but that he has personally and namedly claimed you as his own.
elements.questionHint: God says "I call you by name" right before "you are mine." Why might being called by name, rather than just being part of a group he owns, matter for how secure this belonging feels?

elements.passageText: <sup>19</sup> So then you are no longer foreigners and noncitizens, but you are fellow citizens with the saints and members of God’s household,

elements.question: What else should we remind ourselves of instead?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: Paul uses political and household language to describe belonging: no longer "foreigners and noncitizens," but "fellow citizens with the saints" and "members of God's household." Both images describe full, settled belonging rather than a provisional or outsider status — a citizen has rights and standing that a foreigner doesn't, and a household member lives inside the family rather than visiting from outside. The word "no longer" implies a real change in status, not just a feeling; something true before, being foreign and not belonging, has been replaced by full membership. Remembering this means recalling that you're not on the outside looking in — you actually live inside the household now.
elements.questionHint: Paul uses two images — citizenship and household membership — instead of just saying "you belong." What does each of those specifically add that a vaguer statement of belonging wouldn't capture?

elements.passageText: <sup>9</sup> But you are a chosen race, a royal priesthood, a holy nation, a people of his own, so that you may proclaim the virtues of the one who called you out of darkness into his marvelous light.

elements.question: What else should we remind ourselves of instead?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: Peter stacks up identity after identity — "a chosen race, a royal priesthood, a holy nation, a people of his own" — each phrase emphasizing that this belonging was God's initiative and choice, not something worked toward. And it comes with a purpose: "so that you may proclaim the virtues of the one who called you out of darkness into his marvelous light." Belonging here isn't just a private comfort to hold onto quietly; it's tied to being called out of darkness for the specific purpose of telling others about it. Remembering this identity means remembering both that you were chosen and claimed, and that this claiming has something to say through you.

elements.question: Tell Stanley a better story ...
elements.answer:
Aged 11, Stanley saw the look in his father’s eyes - the anger and disgust as he looked at those people. Stanley never wanted his father to look at him that way, and this fear shaped him. Unconsciously he began to fear that maybe he was a waster and that his dad would look at him with those eyes. He put his hope in hard work to win his dad’s respect. As a teenager he avoided TV, or going out with his mates. He worked late on the farm. He feared that if his dad ever really saw him, he’d see him as a waster, and look at him with those eyes. Hard work became his only hope. He spent the rest of his life running from that look. When he married and had kids, he loved them dearly, but he was still running. If he stopped to play with the kids, or take his wife out, his dad’s look would chase him. The farm was the only safe place. Stanley was hiding from himself, from everyone - scared that they would see him as a waster. Scared of those eyes. Yes, Stanley would look at Christ, but he was scared to let Christ look deep into his soul. To flourish, he needs to let Jesus in. He needs to watch Jesus take his 11-year-old self by the hand, as He speaks these words:

Your father loves you to bits. He has been through a lot and he is hurting. He has worked so hard his whole life and money has always been tight. He wanted to provide enough for his family, but when he couldn’t he began to hate himself, and in his pain, bitterness started to grow towards others who had an easy life. One day you saw that bitterness in his eyes, when he looked at those people in the fancy cars on the way to the football. That day you saw a look that left a scar on your soul. You feared that one day your dad would look at you that same way. But Stanley, I want you to see past the look and see your father’s pain. That look was not about you, it was about his struggles. In his pain, bitterness got a foothold, and that day it jumped from his eyes into your soul and you have been running ever since. That bitterness has put shadows in your soul and in your family. It has cost you peace in your soul, peace in your family, and it will cost you your farm. Your worth is not measured by how much you work. Your father loves you and your Heavenly Father loves you, I love you. I see your pain and I see your brokenness, I see the darkness in your soul that you are scared to look at, and I want to make this my home. I am here, in your heart to stay. I want you to see my eyes, as I look on you. I see the beauty within brokenness, you are loved, we are home, you don’t need to run any more.

When Stanley allows Jesus to gaze on him, he can stop running from his father’s eyes. He can spend time with the people he loves, enjoying the eyes of grace.

elements.question: mid-30s
elements.answer:
Andrew has been following Christ for the last five years. Before coming to faith, he lived a life that he’s not proud of. His past is filled with mistakes, including broken relationships, wasted opportunities, substance abuse, and decisions that hurt others. When Andrew accepted Christ, he experienced a massive sense of forgiveness and hope. For the first time in years, he felt free from his guilt and shame. He was baptised, and his church welcomed him warmly, reminding him that he is now a child of God.

However, as time has passed, Andrew has struggled to fully embrace his new identity. He finds himself haunted by memories of his past and feels that others, especially those who knew him before he became a Christian, still see him as the same old person. Although he is growing in his faith, reading the Bible, and attending church, Andrew sometimes feels like his old life is following him around. He wonders, ‘Am I really that different? Or am I just pretending to have changed?’

Andrew often feels discouraged, especially when he faces temptations or falls into old habits of thinking - or worse, when he relapses into old sins. (He is thankful this is becoming less frequent - but regularly depressed that he still falls into some of his old ways of behaving.)

He knows in his head that he has been born again, and is a child of God and a new creation in Christ - but his heart finds it difficult to believe that his past no longer defines him.
