elements.passageText: <sup>26</sup> I will give you a new heart, and I will put a new spirit within you. I will remove the heart of stone from your body and give you a heart of flesh.

elements.question: What are some of the ways we are ’new’ in Christ?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: God promises a new heart and a new spirit, and specifically the removal of a heart of stone and its replacement with a heart of flesh. This is a deep, inward newness — not a change of behavior alone but a total replacement of the disposition underneath our behavior. A heart of stone can't feel, respond, or soften; a heart of flesh can. Being new in Christ means our capacity to love God and others, to be moved by what moves him, has been given to us fresh — it wasn't there before, and we couldn't manufacture it ourselves.
elements.questionHint: What's the difference between a heart of stone and a heart of flesh — what can one do that the other can't?

elements.passageText: <sup>4</sup> Therefore we have been buried with him through baptism into death, in order that just as Christ was raised from the dead through the glory of the Father, so we too may live a new life.

elements.question: What are some of the ways we are ’new’ in Christ?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: Paul ties our newness to Christ's resurrection: because we were buried with him through baptism into death, we are raised to "live a new life," patterned after the way Christ was raised "through the glory of the Father." This isn't self-improvement; it's a death-and-resurrection reality applied to us. The old life ended in a real sense — buried — and what continues now is a genuinely new kind of existence, empowered by the same glory that raised Jesus. Our newness, then, has resurrection power behind it, not just good intentions.
elements.questionHint: What does Paul say happened to us "through baptism" before he mentions living a "new life" — what had to happen first?

elements.passageText: <sup>17</sup> So then, if anyone is in Christ, he is a new creation; what is old has passed away – look, what is new has come!

elements.question: What are some of the ways we are ’new’ in Christ?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: This verse states it as plainly as possible: anyone in Christ "is a new creation" — not improved, not patched up, but new. "What is old has passed away — look, what is new has come!" The exclamation captures the sense of surprise and wonder Paul wants us to feel; this is a category change, like the difference between the old creation and the new one God is making. Being in Christ doesn't just add something to who we were — it marks the old identity as finished and gone.
elements.questionHint: What two contrasting words does Paul use for what the old has done and what the new has done — what kind of change do those words suggest?

elements.passageText: <sup>5</sup> he saved us not by works of righteousness that we have done but on the basis of his mercy, through the washing of the new birth and the renewing of the Holy Spirit,

elements.question: What are some of the ways we are ’new’ in Christ?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: Here the newness comes through "the washing of the new birth and the renewing of the Holy Spirit," and Paul is careful to say this happened "not by works of righteousness that we have done but on the basis of his mercy." So one way we are new is that we've been washed and reborn — cleansed and given a fresh start — and this newness is entirely the Spirit's doing, not something we earned by good behavior. It's mercy that makes us new, and the Spirit who keeps renewing us afterward.
elements.questionHint: According to this verse, what does Paul say did NOT produce our new birth — and what did, instead?

elements.passageText: <sup>3</sup> Blessed be the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ! By his great mercy he gave us new birth into a living hope through the resurrection of Jesus Christ from the dead,

elements.question: What are some of the ways we are ’new’ in Christ?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: Peter connects our newness to hope: "he gave us new birth into a living hope through the resurrection of Jesus Christ from the dead." So one way we're new is that we're not just new people, we're new people with a living hope — a hope with life in it, because it rests on a resurrection that actually happened. This new birth isn't abstract; it's grounded in "great mercy" and produces real, forward-looking hope rather than a vague optimism, because the same power that raised Jesus stands behind it.
elements.questionHint: What word does Peter use to describe the kind of "hope" this new birth gives us, and what event does he say it comes "through"?

elements.passageText: <sup>20</sup> I have been crucified with Christ, and it is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me. So the life I now live in the body, I live because of the faithfulness of the Son of God, who loved me and gave himself for me.

elements.question: What are some of the ways we are ’new’ in Christ?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: Paul describes his newness almost paradoxically: "I have been crucified with Christ, and it is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me." Being new means the old "I" — the one running the show before — has been put to death, and now Christ himself lives in and through him. Yet Paul doesn't disappear; he still lives "in the body," but the life he lives now flows from "the faithfulness of the Son of God, who loved me and gave himself for me." Newness here means a new source and motive for living, not just new behavior.
elements.questionHint: Paul says it's "no longer I who live" — so who does he say is now living in him, and what does that change about where his life comes from?

elements.text: Jesus does not just ’patch us up.’ The corruption we face, because of sin, is much bigger than any ’patch-up’ could fix. But thankfully, the salvation Jesus brings to us is even greater than the depths of our sin.

elements.passageText: <sup>3</sup> Jesus replied, “I tell you the solemn truth, unless a person is born from above, he cannot see the kingdom of God.”

elements.question: Why is it so important that we are made new in Christ?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: Jesus makes it a matter of ability, not preference: "unless a person is born from above, he cannot see the kingdom of God." Being made new isn't a bonus add-on to a spiritually healthy life — Jesus says it's the one thing without which the kingdom of God simply cannot be seen at all. That word "cannot" is stark; no amount of effort, morality, or religious activity substitutes for it. Being made new in Christ matters this much because it's the very thing that opens our eyes to see and enter what God is doing.
elements.questionHint: What verb does Jesus use to describe what someone "cannot" do without being born from above — what does that imply about trying to get into the kingdom any other way?

elements.text: Sin is big, but salvation is bigger. That’s why we need a radical new start. But we must be clear: God doesn’t love us because we are good - it’s the other way round: God makes us good because He loves us.

elements.passageText: <sup>3</sup> for you have died and your life is hidden with Christ in God. <sup>5</sup> So put to death whatever in your nature belongs to the earth: sexual immorality, impurity, shameful passion, evil desire, and greed which is idolatry.

elements.question: Is our old self something that is dead, or needs to die, or both?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: Both, and the passage holds these together without smoothing out the tension. Verse 3 states a fact already true: "you have died and your life is hidden with Christ in God" — in Christ, our old self's claim on us is already over. But verse 5 commands action: "put to death whatever in your nature belongs to the earth," naming things like sexual immorality, impurity, shameful passion, evil desire, and greed. So our old self is legally and spiritually dead already, but we still have to actively kill off its remaining influence in how we live day to day.
elements.questionHint: Verse 3 says something already happened ("you have died") — so why does verse 5 still give a command to "put to death" anything, if it's already dead?

elements.text: Christ died for us, in our place, to bring us to God. He was raised from the dead, to begin a new creation, and to make us new. We have not yet been taken to the New Heavens and the New Earth. We still live in this present evil age. That’s why there is a call, as well as a proclamation: we need to keep putting to death the old nature that is now dead through Christ. We are to be as different from our old selves as light is from darkness - and yet this difference does not happen by remote control. We are called to take an active part in the transformation.

elements.passageText: <sup>9</sup> Do not lie to one another since you have put off the old man with its practices <sup>10</sup> and have been clothed with the new man that is being renewed in knowledge according to the image of the one who created it.

elements.question: What are some of the ’old’ things we are to get rid of?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: Paul first singles out lying — "Do not lie to one another" — as something that belongs to what "you have put off," the old man with its practices. The old self isn't just a vague concept; it has specific habits, and dishonesty with each other is one Paul calls out by name. In its place, we've been "clothed with the new man that is being renewed in knowledge according to the image of the one who created it" — so getting rid of the old isn't just subtraction, it's replacement with a self being remade to look like God again.
elements.questionHint: What specific practice does Paul name as belonging to "the old man," right before describing what we've put on instead?

elements.passageText: <sup>6</sup> We know that our old man was crucified with him so that the body of sin would no longer dominate us, so that we would no longer be enslaved to sin.

elements.question: What are some of the ’old’ things we are to get rid of?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: Paul names "our old man" as the thing that "was crucified with him" — Christ's crucifixion, applied to us, put our former self to death. The purpose clause tells us why: "so that the body of sin would no longer dominate us, so that we would no longer be enslaved to sin." What's gotten rid of, specifically, is sin's domination and our slavery to it — not that sin's presence vanishes overnight, but its ruling power over us has been broken because the old self that answered to it is dead.
elements.questionHint: What two things does Paul say the crucifixion of "our old man" was meant to end — look at the "so that" phrases.

elements.passageText: <sup>24</sup> Now those who belong to Christ have crucified the flesh with its passions and desires.

elements.question: What are some of the ’old’ things we are to get rid of?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: Paul says plainly what those who belong to Christ have done: "crucified the flesh with its passions and desires." The old things to get rid of are named as "passions and desires" belonging to the flesh — not just outward sins but the inner cravings that produce them. And the verb is crucifixion, not gradual improvement or willpower management; it's a decisive, violent putting-to-death that belongs to what it means to be Christ's. Getting rid of the old isn't tidying up; it's execution.
elements.questionHint: What verb does Paul use for what's been done to "the flesh with its passions and desires" — what does that word suggest about how decisive this is?

elements.text: The very centre of who we are is being renewed, so that we take on the character of Christ. New birth doesn’t ’improve’ our old nature, it gives us a new nature, a new capacity to put on Christ.

elements.passageText: <sup>22</sup> You were taught with reference to your former way of life to lay aside the old man who is being corrupted in accordance with deceitful desires, <sup>23</sup> to be renewed in the spirit of your mind, <sup>24</sup> and to put on the new man who has been created in God’s image – in righteousness and holiness that comes from truth.

elements.question: What are we to put on instead?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: After laying aside "the old man who is being corrupted in accordance with deceitful desires," Paul describes two things that follow: being "renewed in the spirit of your mind," and putting on "the new man who has been created in God's image — in righteousness and holiness that comes from truth." So what we put on instead is a renewed mind and a new self modeled on God's own image, marked specifically by righteousness and holiness that comes from truth rather than the deceit that marked the old way of life.
elements.questionHint: What two qualities does Paul say mark the "new man," and what does he say those qualities "come from"?

elements.passageText: <sup>8</sup> But sin, seizing the opportunity through the commandment, produced in me all kinds of wrong desires. For apart from the law, sin is dead.

elements.question: What are we to put on instead?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: This verse looks at it from the angle of the law and sin's opportunism: "sin, seizing the opportunity through the commandment, produced in me all kinds of wrong desires." Paul isn't describing something we put on here so much as exposing how sin uses even good commands as a foothold to stir up desires we wouldn't otherwise have noticed. The lesson for what we put on instead comes by contrast — recognizing this trap is part of learning to live by something other than law-triggered sin, a life the rest of Romans describes as walking "in the Spirit."
elements.questionHint: What does Paul say sin used as its "opportunity" to produce wrong desires in him — what does that tell you about where the danger actually comes from?

elements.passageText: <sup>2</sup> Do not be conformed to this present world, but be transformed by the renewing of your mind, so that you may test and approve what is the will of God – what is good and well-pleasing and perfect.

elements.question: What are we to put on instead?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: Paul contrasts two postures: "Do not be conformed to this present world, but be transformed by the renewing of your mind." What we put on instead of the old patterns is transformation — a mind actively being renewed rather than passively shaped by the world around us. And the purpose isn't renewal for its own sake: it's "so that you may test and approve what is the will of God — what is good and well-pleasing and perfect." A renewed mind is what lets us actually recognize and embrace God's will instead of just going along with everyone else's default settings.
elements.questionHint: What two opposite verbs does Paul use — one for what not to be, one for what to be — and what gets renewed in the second one?

elements.passageText: <sup>10</sup> For we are his workmanship, having been created in Christ Jesus for good works that God prepared beforehand so we may do them.

elements.question: What are we to put on instead?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: Paul says we are "his workmanship, created in Christ Jesus for good works that God prepared beforehand so we may do them." What we put on instead of the old self is a life of good works — not works we invent to earn favor, but ones God already planned out ahead of time for us to walk into. Being new means being God's own handiwork, shaped with a purpose already in mind, so that doing good isn't a burden added on top of our identity but the natural outworking of what we were made new for.

elements.question: Living out his new identity ...
elements.answer:
Being made new in Christ is not a minor adjustment - it’s a total transformation. Anyone who is in Christ is a ’new creation.’ The old has gone, and the new has come. This means that Andrew is no longer defined by the mistakes he made in his past. Andrew needs to meditate on these truths until they dwell within him and begin to shape him. But this new life doesn’t happen automatically, without effort. For Andrew, this means recognising that his past mistakes no longer define him, but it also means actively working to let go of the habits, mindsets, and behaviours that belonged to his old life.

Andrew feels like his past is still following him around, but this is exactly why the Bible tells us to continually ’put off’ the old self and ’put on’ the new self. Every time Andrew resists temptations to fall into old patterns, he is living out his new identity in Christ. This doesn’t mean the old struggles will disappear instantly, but it does mean that Andrew has the power, through the Holy Spirit, to walk in newness of life.

Andrew needs to internalise the truth that God’s work in him is ongoing. He may still feel the weight of his past and the pull of old habits, but God is continually at work transforming him to be more like Christ. He can take comfort in knowing that being a new creation is not about never making mistakes - it’s about living in the assurance that God’s grace enables him to keep growing. God will never abandon him. He is faithfully working in Andrew’s life, even when progress feels slow.

Andrew can take steps to help himself fully embrace his new identity: Dwelling in the truth of God’s Word, especially the truth of his new identity in Christ, will help that truth dwell in him. Andrew might also benefit from connecting with a Christian mentor or accountability partner who can encourage him in his walk and remind him of his new identity when he’s feeling discouraged. Having someone to pray with and share struggles with can really help. Andrew needs to consciously surrender any lingering shame from his past to God. He can do this through prayer, asking God to help him release the weight of his old mistakes and to live in the freedom of being forgiven and made new. Each time Andrew chooses to live in a way that reflects his new identity - whether it’s showing kindness, resisting temptation, or making choices that honour God - he is ’putting on’ the new self. He can look for ways to actively practice living out this new creation, asking God for strength each day. His new life is a reflection of the resurrection power that raised Jesus from the dead.

elements.question: late 20s
elements.answer:
Hannah has been a believer for most of her life. She attends church regularly, listens to sermons, and volunteers for occasional events. But even though she has been involved for years, Hannah often feels like she doesn’t really belong in her church community. She’s friendly with people at church, but she hasn’t formed any deep relationships. Sometimes, she wonders if anyone would even notice if she stopped attending.

Recently, Hannah has been wrestling with a growing sense of isolation. While she enjoys her personal relationship with Christ, she has been noticing more and more that she doesn’t feel deeply connected to her church family. Every Sunday, she hears about being part of the body of Christ, but in practice, she feels like a distant spectator. When her pastor talks about community and serving one another, Hannah feels guilty for not being more involved, but she also feels unsure about how to take the next step. ’Isn’t it enough to just come to church and be a good Christian?’ she asks herself.

Hannah wants to experience the kind of deep, meaningful relationships she hears about in the Bible, but she isn’t sure how to make that happen.

elements.text:
Being a member of a local church is no optional extra for Christians. It is essential to our identity as followers of Christ.

As disciples of Christ, we are bound to Christ, and therefore bound to one another in the love of God; our lives are intertwined as we seek to follow Christ together.

elements.passageText: <sup>12</sup> For just as the body is one and yet has many members, and all the members of the body – though many – are one body, so too is Christ. <sup>13</sup> For in one Spirit we were all baptized into one body. Whether Jews or Greeks or slaves or free, we were all made to drink of the one Spirit. <sup>14</sup> For in fact the body is not a single member, but many.

elements.question: What does it mean to be a member of Christ’s body?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: Paul draws a direct comparison: "just as the body is one and yet has many members... so too is Christ." Being a member means belonging to a single body made of many distinct parts, united by one baptism into "one Spirit" — a unity that crosses categories that might otherwise divide people: "Jews or Greeks or slaves or free." And crucially, "the body is not a single member, but many" — so being a member of Christ's body means neither standing alone as your own body nor being swallowed into sameness, but being one distinct part among many, joined by the same Spirit.
elements.questionHint: What does Paul say the Spirit did to unite people who would otherwise be divided by categories like Jew/Greek or slave/free?

elements.passageText: <sup>4</sup> For just as in one body we have many members, and not all the members serve the same function, <sup>5</sup> so we who are many are one body in Christ, and individually we are members who belong to one another.

elements.question: What does it mean to be a member of Christ’s body?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: Paul makes the same body analogy but adds a detail: "not all the members serve the same function." Being a member of Christ's body means having a distinct role — not everyone does the same thing — while still being genuinely "one body in Christ." And then comes the relational payoff: "individually we are members who belong to one another." Membership isn't just about function or belonging to Christ in the abstract; it means we belong to each other, with real obligations and connections between the parts.
elements.questionHint: Besides belonging to Christ, who else does Paul say we "belong to" as members — look at the last phrase of verse 5.

elements.passageText: <sup>11</sup> It was he who gave some as apostles, some as prophets, some as evangelists, and some as pastors and teachers, <sup>12</sup> to equip the saints for the work of ministry, that is, to build up the body of Christ, <sup>13</sup> until we all attain to the unity of the faith and of the knowledge of the Son of God – a mature person, attaining to the measure of Christ’s full stature.

elements.question: What does it mean to be a member of Christ’s body?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: Here membership connects to growth: Christ gave some "as apostles, some as prophets, some as evangelists, and some as pastors and teachers, to equip the saints for the work of ministry." Being a member means having gifted people placed among us specifically "to build up the body of Christ" — membership isn't static, it's meant to move us "until we all attain to the unity of the faith... a mature person, attaining to the measure of Christ's full stature." So being part of the body means being equipped and grown toward maturity, together, not left to figure it out alone.
elements.questionHint: What is the stated purpose ("to build up...") behind the gifted people Christ gave to the church?

elements.text: Bodies are interdependent, not independent. If you saw a severed ear lying on the road, you would not think, ‘Oh, look! There’s an independent ear, striking out on its own. Good for it!’ You would recognise that there had been some tragedy. Ears do not do well lying ’independently’ on the road. elements.passageText: <sup>19</sup> So then you are no longer foreigners and noncitizens, but you are fellow citizens with the saints and members of God’s household, <sup>20</sup> because you have been built on the foundation of the apostles and prophets, with Christ Jesus himself as the cornerstone. <sup>21</sup> In him the whole building, being joined together, grows into a holy temple in the Lord, <sup>22</sup> in whom you also are being built together into a dwelling place of God in the Spirit.

elements.question: What does it mean to belong to the household of God?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: Paul first strikes a contrast: "you are no longer foreigners and noncitizens, but you are fellow citizens with the saints and members of God's household." Belonging to God's household means a status change — from outsider to family member. And this household has structure: it's "built on the foundation of the apostles and prophets, with Christ Jesus himself as the cornerstone," growing into "a holy temple in the Lord" where God himself dwells "in the Spirit." So belonging isn't just membership in a group; it's being built into something alive, with Christ holding the whole structure together and God actually living within it.
elements.questionHint: What does Paul say we've gone from being ("foreigners and noncitizens") to being instead — and who does he say the "cornerstone" of this household is?

elements.passageText: <sup>5</sup> you yourselves, as living stones, are built up as a spiritual house to be a holy priesthood and to offer spiritual sacrifices that are acceptable to God through Jesus Christ.

elements.question: What does it mean to belong to the household of God?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: Peter calls believers "living stones" who "are built up as a spiritual house" with a specific purpose: "to be a holy priesthood and to offer spiritual sacrifices that are acceptable to God through Jesus Christ." Belonging to God's household here means being actively used — not decorative stones but living ones, built into something functional, with a priestly job to do. And the sacrifices we offer aren't animals or grain but something spiritual, made acceptable "through Jesus Christ" rather than through our own merit.
elements.questionHint: Peter calls us "living stones" being built into what kind of house — and what job does that house's occupants, a "holy priesthood," have?

elements.passageText: <sup>6</sup> But Christ is faithful as a son over God’s house. We are of his house, if in fact we hold firmly to our confidence and the hope we take pride in.

elements.question: What does it mean to belong to the household of God?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: The writer contrasts Moses, a servant "in" God's house, with Christ who is "faithful as a son over God's house." Belonging here comes with a condition attached: "We are of his house, if in fact we hold firmly to our confidence and the hope we take pride in." So belonging to God's household means being under a faithful Son rather than merely a servant, but it's a belonging meant to be held onto — sustained by continuing confidence and hope, not just a one-time membership card.
elements.questionHint: What condition does the writer attach to being "of his house" — what are we told to "hold firmly" to?

elements.text: We often first turn to Christ individually, in repentance and faith. But we are not called to follow Christ individually. We are part of something greater, a household built on the foundation of Christ. This household is where we learn what it means to love and be loved, to serve and be served.

elements.passageText: <sup>9</sup> But you are a chosen race, a royal priesthood, a holy nation, a people of his own, so that you may proclaim the virtues of the one who called you out of darkness into his marvelous light. <sup>10</sup> You once were not a people , but now you are God’s people. You were shown no mercy, but now you have received mercy.

elements.question: How does our identity as a royal priesthood affect our mission?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: Peter stacks up titles — "a chosen race, a royal priesthood, a holy nation, a people of his own" — and then states the purpose behind all of them: "so that you may proclaim the virtues of the one who called you out of darkness into his marvelous light." Our identity isn't just status; it comes with a job — to broadcast what God is like, based on what he's done for us personally. And that mission is rooted in a real change: "You once were not a people, but now you are God's people," shown mercy where there was none.
elements.questionHint: What is the stated purpose ("so that...") behind being called "a royal priesthood" — what are we supposed to do because of that identity?

elements.passageText: <sup>6</sup> and has appointed us as a kingdom, as priests serving his God and Father – to him be the glory and the power for ever and ever! Amen.

elements.question: How does our identity as a royal priesthood affect our mission?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: This verse is short but points the same direction: Christ "has appointed us as a kingdom, as priests serving his God and Father." Our priestly identity isn't self-appointed status to enjoy privately — it comes from being "appointed," and it's oriented toward service, "serving his God and Father." The verse ends not with a call to action for us but with worship — "to him be the glory and the power for ever and ever" — which suggests that our priestly mission ultimately exists to point back to God's glory, not our own.
elements.questionHint: Who does the verse say "appointed" us as a kingdom and priests, and what does the verse conclude by giving to him?

elements.passageText: <sup>5</sup> And now, if you will diligently listen to me and keep my covenant, then you will be my special possession out of all the nations, for all the earth is mine, <sup>6</sup> and you will be to me a kingdom of priests and a holy nation.’ These are the words that you will speak to the Israelites.”

elements.question: How does our identity as a royal priesthood affect our mission?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: This is the original promise the priesthood language echoes: if Israel would "diligently listen" and "keep my covenant," they would be God's "special possession out of all the nations" and "a kingdom of priests and a holy nation." Being a royal priesthood, even here at the root, is conditioned on listening and covenant-keeping, and it comes with a global backdrop — "all the earth is mine" — meaning this special role exists within, and for the sake of, God's purposes for the whole earth, not as a private privilege set apart from everyone else.
elements.questionHint: What two conditions does God attach to Israel becoming "a kingdom of priests" — "if you will diligently listen" and what else?

elements.text: We are called to embody God’s presence in the world. We are called to make him known, bridging the gap between heaven and earth. We are called to proclaim the good news of reconciliation to all creation and to serve as representatives of His kingdom in everyday life.

elements.question: Living a better truth ...
elements.answer:
Hannah needs to know that she already has a place in the body of Christ. The body of Christ is made up of many members, and each is vital to the whole. Hannah may feel like a spectator, but in reality, she is an indispensable part of Christ’s body, simply by virtue of her faith in Christ. Her feelings don’t change the truth that she belongs. Hannah’s life is intertwined with the lives of other believers. She is connected to the church in a deep, spiritual way, even when she doesn’t feel it.

There are different possible reasons why Hannah is struggling to connect. The problem might be (mostly) on her side. Perhaps she hasn’t fully embraced the idea that being part of the body of Christ means active participation, not just passive attendance. She could explore how her gifts can serve the body. Or it might be that she hasn’t taken the time (or doesn’t know how) to develop genuine, Christ-centred relationships where she and others can encourage and strengthen one another. Hannah could make progress by joining a small group or inviting a fellow church member for a meal. Building meaningful relationships takes time, but as Hannah invests in her church community, she will begin to see how those connections deepen her sense of belonging. As she shifts her focus to actively participating and serving, Hannah will likely experience the joy that comes from living out her calling as a member of Christ’s body. By serving others, she will begin to see how God uses her to bless the church and fulfil His mission in the world.

It is also worth acknowledging that the problems may be less (or, at least, not completely) on Hannah’s side. Some church communities are structured in a way that makes it hard for at least some people to integrate well. Perhaps the church community is not very good at integrating newcomers, or single people, or couples without children, or older people, or foreigners, or those from a different background to everyone else. Problems like this are not always easy to see, and nor are they quick to fix (and Hannah may not be in a position to fix them). It is never a good idea to jump to the conclusion that the problem in a situation lies wholly (or mostly) with someone else, and not with us, although it is worth Hannah being aware that in some circumstances a church community may not be structured in such a way that it can easily accommodate and integrate people like her. Being a member of the body of Christ is both a gift and a responsibility. It is a gift both to the individuals and the community, and a responsibility upon both the individuals and the community.

elements.question: early 30s
elements.answer:
David is passionate about his faith and actively involved in his church. He attends Bible studies, volunteers regularly, and leads a small group. On Sundays, David feels close to God and is encouraged by his identity in Christ. But when Monday comes, and he returns to work, that sense of identity fades.

David works as a marketing manager for a large company. The working environment is competitive and high-pressure. His colleagues often use underhanded tactics to get ahead, and there is a strong emphasis on success and performance. David struggles to live out his faith. He finds himself cutting corners, exaggerating results, sometimes telling outright falsehoods, and going along with office gossip just to fit in and avoid conflict. By the end of the working week, David feels drained and guilty, knowing that he isn’t living as the person God has called him to be.

David wants to be the same person at work as he is at church, but he feels stuck. He wonders, ‘How can I live out who I am in Christ, in a place where success seems to come at the cost of integrity?’ He wonders if it is even possible to reflect Christ in his actions when everyone else is playing by different rules.

elements.text: The Christian life is about embodying the values of the kingdom of God in our everyday lives. We uncover who we are in Christ through our actions. You must choose to live out who you are in Christ. It is a daily decision to trust Him, no matter what the circumstances.

elements.passageText: <sup>10</sup> Don’t be afraid, for I am with you! Don’t be frightened, for I am your God! I strengthen you – yes, I help you – yes, I uphold you with my saving right hand!

elements.question: What can help us trust God, no matter the circumstances?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: The verse gives one direct reason not to fear: God's own presence — "for I am with you!" Trusting God in hard circumstances doesn't start with fixing the circumstances; it starts with the assurance that God himself is present in them. The command "don't be afraid" isn't wishful thinking, it's grounded in that stated fact. When circumstances feel overwhelming, the passage's answer for what can help us trust is remarkably simple and personal: God saying, in effect, "I am here with you, so you don't have to face this alone."
elements.questionHint: What reason does God give right after saying "Don't be afraid" — what four words state why?

elements.text: The Christian life is a process. We grow in our faith, we reflect Christ more and more in our lives, we learn to walk as he walked.

elements.passageText: <sup>4</sup> Therefore we have been buried with him through baptism into death, in order that just as Christ was raised from the dead through the glory of the Father, so we too may live a new life.

elements.question: What does it mean to walk in newness of life?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: Walking in newness of life is rooted in a burial and a resurrection: "we have been buried with him through baptism into death, in order that just as Christ was raised from the dead through the glory of the Father, so we too may live a new life." To walk in newness means our daily life now runs on resurrection power, not on the old patterns that were buried with Christ. It's not a fresh start we generate ourselves — it's a life that flows out of the same glory that raised Jesus from the dead, made ours through union with him.
elements.questionHint: What does Paul say happened to us "through baptism" before he mentions the "new life" — what had to happen first?

elements.passageText: <sup>16</sup> But I say, live by the Spirit and you will not carry out the desires of the flesh. <sup>17</sup> For the flesh has desires that are opposed to the Spirit, and the Spirit has desires that are opposed to the flesh, for these are in opposition to each other, so that you cannot do what you want. <sup>18</sup> But if you are led by the Spirit, you are not under the law.

elements.question: What does it mean to walk in newness of life?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: Paul frames it as a walk empowered by the Spirit: "live by the Spirit and you will not carry out the desires of the flesh." Walking in newness means engaging in an ongoing conflict — "the flesh has desires that are opposed to the Spirit, and the Spirit has desires that are opposed to the flesh" — so that we can't simply do whatever we want by default. But being "led by the Spirit" changes our relationship to the law itself: "you are not under the law." Newness of life, then, is a Spirit-led walk that actually counters the flesh's pull, not just willpower against it.
elements.questionHint: What does Paul say we will NOT carry out if we "live by the Spirit" — and what's opposing what in verse 17?

elements.passageText: <sup>22</sup> You were taught with reference to your former way of life to lay aside the old man who is being corrupted in accordance with deceitful desires, <sup>23</sup> to be renewed in the spirit of your mind, <sup>24</sup> and to put on the new man who has been created in God’s image – in righteousness and holiness that comes from truth.

elements.question: What does it mean to walk in newness of life?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: This walk has three movements: laying aside "the old man who is being corrupted in accordance with deceitful desires," being "renewed in the spirit of your mind," and putting on "the new man who has been created in God's image." Walking in newness of life means an ongoing process — laying off, renewing, putting on — rather than a single event we complete once. And the goal is specific: righteousness and holiness "that comes from truth," a pointed contrast to the "deceitful desires" that marked the old way of walking.
elements.questionHint: What three actions does Paul describe in order — lay aside, be renewed, and then what?

elements.text: Living out our identity in Christ means integrating that identity into our thoughts and actions. To be the kind of people God wants us to be, we must reflect His character in our lives.

elements.passageText: <sup>15</sup> but, like the Holy One who called you, become holy yourselves in all of your conduct, <sup>16</sup> for it is written, “ You shall be holy , because I am holy .”

elements.question: How does personal holiness reflect our new identity?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: Peter roots our holiness directly in God's own character: "like the Holy One who called you, become holy yourselves in all of your conduct," quoting the command "You shall be holy, because I am holy." Personal holiness isn't an arbitrary rule to follow; it's meant to reflect the very nature of the one who called us. Because we belong to a holy God, holiness in "all of your conduct" — not just select areas — becomes the natural, expected shape of a life that actually matches its new identity as his.
elements.questionHint: Whose character does Peter say our holiness is supposed to match — look at who is called "the Holy One."

elements.passageText: <sup>12</sup> Therefore, as the elect of God, holy and dearly loved, clothe yourselves with a heart of mercy, kindness, humility, gentleness, and patience, <sup>13</sup> bearing with one another and forgiving one another, if someone happens to have a complaint against anyone else. Just as the Lord has forgiven you, so you also forgive others. <sup>14</sup> And to all these virtues add love, which is the perfect bond.

elements.question: How does personal holiness reflect our new identity?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: Paul describes holiness less as rule-keeping and more as clothing: "as the elect of God, holy and dearly loved, clothe yourselves with a heart of mercy, kindness, humility, gentleness, and patience." Because we're already called "holy and dearly loved," what follows is bearing with one another and forgiving "just as the Lord has forgiven you" — holiness reflected outward in relationships, not just private virtue. And "add love, which is the perfect bond" ties it all together, showing that holiness expressed toward others, held together by love, is what our new identity looks like in practice.
elements.questionHint: What does Paul say to "clothe yourselves with," and what's the one thing added at the end that binds all those virtues together?

elements.passageText: <sup>1</sup> Therefore, since we have these promises, dear friends, let us cleanse ourselves from everything that could defile the body and the spirit, and thus accomplish holiness out of reverence for God.

elements.question: How does personal holiness reflect our new identity?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: Paul draws holiness directly out of what God has already promised: "since we have these promises, dear friends, let us cleanse ourselves from everything that could defile the body and the spirit, and thus accomplish holiness out of reverence for God." Holiness here flows from gratitude and reverence, not fear or obligation — it's a response to promises already given, a cleansing that touches both "body and spirit," the whole person. Reflecting our new identity through holiness means letting God's promises to us produce active cleansing, out of reverence, rather than waiting passively for change to happen on its own.
elements.questionHint: What does Paul say we should cleanse ourselves "from" — and what motivation does he give ("out of ___") for pursuing holiness?

elements.text: The gospel is not just about what we believe, but also about how we live. Being who we are in Christ means leaving our comfort zones and sharing His love. Our lives should display that we are in Christ.

elements.passageText: <sup>22</sup> But the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faithfulness, <sup>23</sup> gentleness, and self-control. Against such things there is no law.

elements.question: How do we bear the fruit of the Spirit as part of our new identity?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: Paul lists the fruit as a single unified harvest — "love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faithfulness, gentleness, and self-control" — not separate fruits to pursue individually but "the fruit of the Spirit," singular, produced by the Spirit's presence rather than manufactured by our own effort. And notably, "against such things there is no law" — this kind of life doesn't need external rules to justify or restrain it, because it's already in step with what's good. Bearing this fruit as part of our new identity means letting the Spirit produce this cluster of character in us rather than trying to grow it ourselves.
elements.questionHint: Paul calls this "the fruit of the Spirit" — singular "fruit," not "fruits" — what does that wording suggest about how these qualities show up together?

elements.passageText: <sup>4</sup> Remain in me, and I will remain in you. Just as the branch cannot bear fruit by itself, unless it remains in the vine, so neither can you unless you remain in me. <sup>5</sup> “I am the vine; you are the branches. The one who remains in me – and I in him – bears much fruit, because apart from me you can accomplish nothing.

elements.question: How do we bear the fruit of the Spirit as part of our new identity?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: Jesus makes fruit-bearing entirely dependent on connection: "Remain in me, and I will remain in you... apart from me you can accomplish nothing." Using the vine and branches image, he says a branch can't bear fruit "by itself" — it has to stay attached to the vine. Bearing the fruit of the Spirit as part of our new identity, then, isn't primarily about effort or discipline in isolation; it's about remaining, staying connected to Christ, since he states flatly that fruit only comes from "the one who remains in me — and I in him."
elements.questionHint: What does Jesus say a branch cannot do "by itself" — and what condition does he attach to bearing "much fruit"?

elements.passageText: <sup>8</sup> for you were at one time darkness, but now you are light in the Lord. Walk as children of the light – <sup>9</sup> for the fruit of the light consists in all goodness, righteousness, and truth – <sup>10</sup> trying to learn what is pleasing to the Lord.

elements.question: How do we bear the fruit of the Spirit as part of our new identity?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: Paul frames this as a shift from darkness to light: "you were at one time darkness, but now you are light in the Lord." Bearing fruit here means walking "as children of the light," since "the fruit of the light consists in all goodness, righteousness, and truth." Our new identity as light-bearers naturally produces this fruit as we go, and the ongoing posture is one of discernment — "trying to learn what is pleasing to the Lord" — suggesting bearing fruit is paired with continually learning, not something we master once and finish.
elements.questionHint: What three qualities does Paul say make up "the fruit of the light," and what present-tense activity does he pair with walking in it?

elements.text: As we live out our identity in Christ, as His body, we become the hands and feet of Jesus, bringing His love and compassion into our communities. We engage with the world around us, sharing His truth and love in practical ways.

elements.passageText: <sup>10</sup> For we are his workmanship, having been created in Christ Jesus for good works that God prepared beforehand so we may do them.

elements.question: What else are we to do?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: Paul reminds us again that we are "his workmanship, created in Christ Jesus for good works that God prepared beforehand so we may do them." What else we're to do is walk into good works that were already planned out for us in advance — not works we invent from scratch, but ones prepared ahead of time and waiting for us to do them. Being God's workmanship means our doing flows out of his design, so the "what else" isn't a separate task list but the natural unfolding of who he made us to be.
elements.questionHint: According to this verse, who "prepared beforehand" the good works we're meant to do — and what does that tell you about whose idea they were?

elements.passageText: <sup>23</sup> Whatever you are doing, work at it with enthusiasm, as to the Lord and not for people, <sup>24</sup> because you know that you will receive your inheritance from the Lord as the reward. Serve the Lord Christ.

elements.question: What else are we to do?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: Paul's instruction here is about attitude in whatever we do: "Whatever you are doing, work at it with enthusiasm, as to the Lord and not for people." What else we're to do is bring wholehearted effort to ordinary tasks, reframing who we're really working for — not human approval, but the Lord himself. And there's a promise attached: "you will receive your inheritance from the Lord as the reward," which reorients even mundane work around eternal reward rather than earthly recognition, closing with the simple charge, "Serve the Lord Christ."
elements.questionHint: Paul says to work "as to" whom, "and not for" whom — what's the contrast he's drawing there?

elements.passageText: <sup>58</sup> So then, dear brothers and sisters, be firm. Do not be moved! Always be outstanding in the work of the Lord, knowing that your labor is not in vain in the Lord.

elements.question: What else are we to do?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: Paul calls believers to "be firm. Do not be moved! Always be outstanding in the work of the Lord." What else we're to do is persevere steadily in good work rather than drifting or giving up, and he gives the reason: "you know that your labor is not in vain in the Lord." This assurance — that nothing done for the Lord is wasted, even when results aren't visible yet — is what fuels the firmness and steadiness Paul is calling for, addressed warmly to "dear brothers and sisters" as family, not strangers.

elements.question: David being who he is ...
elements.answer:
David needs to be shaped by the truth that his identity in Christ is constant, no matter his environment. Whether he’s in church or at work, he is a new creation in Christ. His identity doesn’t change based on his surroundings. God calls us to be holy in all areas of life, reflecting His character wherever we go. David’s work environment may tempt him to compromise his values, but his identity in Christ means that he is called to something greater. He is a child of God in all situations.

David’s struggle to live out his identity in Christ at work is understandable - he faces real pressures. But God promises to be with us and strengthen us, even in difficult circumstances. David doesn’t have to face these challenges alone; he can rely on God’s strength to help him stand firm in his identity, even when it’s hard. David can begin to trust that God’s plan for his life includes integrity and faithfulness, even if it doesn’t seem to lead to immediate success by the world’s standards. By trusting God, David can choose to act with honesty and love, knowing that his ultimate reward comes from God, not from his boss or colleagues.

For David, this might mean making small but significant changes in how he interacts with his colleagues. Instead of going along with office gossip, he could choose to speak words that build others up. Instead of cutting corners to meet deadlines, he can commit to doing his work with integrity, trusting that God will honour his faithfulness. God has prepared good works for us to do, and that includes the work we do in our daily lives. David’s job is not just a means to an end - it’s part of his mission as a follower of Christ. By seeing his work as an opportunity to reflect Christ’s love, David can find renewed purpose.

Instead of viewing his workplace as a battleground where he has to compromise to survive, David can see it as a mission field where he is called to be the hands and feet of Jesus. David can shine the light of Christ in a place where it may not be readily visible. David is not responsible for how others respond to that light. Some may be drawn to find out more, others may be provoked to oppose the light. Some people may be intrigued by the difference in how he lives, others may respond with resistance, criticism or even open hostility. If David lives out who he is in Christ, it may help his career, or it may hinder it. He might get promoted because of his integrity, or he might get fired because of it. It is not David’s responsibility to control those outcomes. His responsibility is simple: to be who he is in Christ.
